| `accept_live.sh` after the chain | — | **PASS** (new chat 6.21 s, warm 5.34 s, follow-up 3.7 s) |

`majflt` is the whole-process figure from `/usr/bin/time -v`. **`qwen36` has
no `[MAP]` line to check**: `st_map_shard_range` is on by default only for
`glm53` and `qwen38` (`COLI_MAP_EXPERTS_DEFAULT`), and this engine reads
experts with `st_read_raw` into its own slots, so the `[MAP] … copy=0`
invariant does not apply here.

CLI timings from the same runs, for orientation only — this is not the serving
regime and they are **not** comparable to arm C's 14.84 tok/s / 32.85 s TTFT
(`~/bench/ctx_ladder_out/fk09152356_C.jsonl`, `coli serve` over HTTP): packet
prefill 625 positions in 53.8 s; short prefill 22 positions in 6.3–7.7 s.

### The oracle `qwen36` did not have

`glm53`'s `teacher_forcing` line has no counterpart on this engine, and
`step()` applies the LM head only to the LAST row because that is all decode
needs — so there was nothing to build a per-position KL oracle on. Added, both
off by default: `Q36_TEACHER_FORCING=1` prints the per-position argmax line,
and `Q36_LOGIT_DUMP_ALL=<path>` writes the **same "GLKD" container**
`GLM53_LOGIT_DUMP_ALL` writes (§X2), so `tools/hot-expert/kl_compare.py` and
`gate_kl` read a `qwen36` dump with no change. Implemented as a flag `step()`
honours rather than a second forward function that could diverge, and the head
pass is deliberately the per-row `matmul_d(...,1,...)` rather than the S>1
batched kernel, so the dump's last row is the engine's own vector and not a
differently-ordered one.

**That last claim is checked, not asserted, and the first run of the chain
found it was being checked wrongly.** `generate()` writes `DUMP=` at
`s == n_new-1`, i.e. at a DECODE step, so comparing the dump's last row against
`DUMP=` at `N_NEW=8` compares two different vectors and the leg failed. At
`N_NEW=1` the `DUMP=` vector IS `step()`'s prefill return value — the vector
the engine used to choose the first generated token — and the comparison is
exact and non-circular: **IDENTICAL, 22 positions × 248 320, on both binaries.**

Two more legs of that first run were weaker than they read, both fixed on its
own evidence: the greedy-text leg compared `^Text` in **stderr**, where this
engine prints only the label (`print_decoded` writes the tokens to stdout), so
it was diffing two empty lines — `gate_lib.sh`'s first failure shape, inside a
script that sources `gate_lib.sh`; and the `majflt` pattern never matched
`/usr/bin/time`'s wording and printed `?` six times. The gate now refuses a
text under 8 non-space characters and a prefill under 20 positions.

### The design document's nibble instruction is REFUTED, and the XOR is kept

`V1-STEP0-2026-09-16.md` §(c), §(d) and §(e) instruct that the CUDA tier's
`stage()` XOR 0x88 "must be dropped, not ported" for Vulkan, reading the
shaders' `i4()` as a two's-complement decode. It is not one. **Every Colibri
Vulkan shader decodes `fmt=2/4` as OFFSET BINARY:**

    float i4(uint w, int l) { return float(int((w >> (uint(l)*4u)) & 0xfu) - 8); }
    c/shaders/qmatmul.comp:47, qmatmul_tile.comp:48,
    c/shaders/qmatmul_gate_up.comp:33, qmatmul_gate_up_tile.comp:27

— which `qmatmul_gate_up.comp:10` calls "int4 (nibble-8)" in its own header —
and `c/backend_vulkan.c:912` copies the bytes verbatim. **The CUDA side has the
same convention at its API boundary:** `coli_cuda_tensor_upload` launches
`offset_to_signed_s4`, an XOR 0x88 kernel (`c/backend_cuda.cu:334`, called at
`:1428`), on the device immediately after the H2D copy, and only then does
`weight_at()` sign-extend. §(c) read `weight_at()` and not the upload. `glm53`
hands its `q4` straight to `coli_vk_tensor_ensure` because ITS container is
already offset binary (`c/quant.h` decodes `(b&0xF)-8`); `qwen36`'s is
two's-complement (`c/qwen36.c:1471-1473` sign-extends). So the XOR is a
**container-convention conversion, not a CUDA step**, and dropping it would
offset every expert weight by 8 quanta.

Proved rather than argued, `c/tests/test_qwen36_vk_nibble.c` (host-only, no GPU):

| case | what | result |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | all 256 byte values, both nibbles: XOR 0x88 + the shader's `i4()` vs the engine's own `unpack_int4_to_int8` | **512 / 512 agree** |
| 2 | the same without the XOR | **512 / 512 DISAGREE** — the leg exists so case 1 cannot become vacuously true |
| 3 | a full-size 2048×512 gate matrix, 1 048 576 elements | **0 differ** |

### What was deliberately NOT ported, and why

- **The R4 trunk placement** (`lm_head` / `dnproj` on a device, `qt_place_of`,
  `qt_trunk_offer`): a second, independent mechanism, still CUDA-only. V1's
  scope is the expert tier; these return CPU here.
- **The uploader thread and the LFRU swap.** A Vulkan "upload" is a `memcpy`
  into mapped memory inside `coli_vk_tensor_ensure3` — there is no async copy
  engine to hide behind a background thread — and 40 × 256 int4-gs64 experts
  are ~18.6 GB of payload, so with the whole set resident there is nothing to
  evict. A swapping tier would also make an A/B non-reproducible.
- **`dev_alloc_footprint`'s cudaMalloc granularity curve**, which
  V1-STEP0 §(f) flags as unmeasured on RADV: not ported blind. The planner
  charges payload bytes and the live `coli_vk_mem_budget3` read every 8
  uploads is the authority that stops the fill (glm53's G6 rule, 1.0 GB
  reserve, `COLI_VK_TIER_RESERVE_GB`). `qt_stats()` prints the planned and the
  driver-reported figure side by side so the gap is a number and not an
  assumption.

### Counts re-derived here, not copied

V1-STEP0 §(f) asks for the qwen36 C-test count to be taken from the tree at
build time. The chain greps the Makefile for it: **13** targets
(`cache_index`, `ctx`, `dense_batch`, `json_escape`, `tok_merges`, the seven
`tier_*`, and this branch's `vk_nibble`), all 13 pass on the rig
(gcc -O3 -march=native, OpenMP) and on the Mac (clang, single-threaded, run
from `c/`). The step-0 estimate was "at least eight".

### V1 step 2 — the tier ON: every expert of the 40 × 256 set resident on dev3, numerics at the oracle's floor, decode **+45.6 %** and TTFT **−67.8 %** (conservative) against the same binary with the tier off, and the arm C floor beaten by **+44 to +48 %**. GATE PASS.

Two chains, both through `run_chain.sh`:
`tools/hot-expert/v1_step2a_chain.sh` (correctness, run `v1s2a09160809`,
08:09–08:16 UTC) and `tools/hot-expert/v1_step2b_chain.sh` (performance, run
`v1s2b09160831`, 08:31–08:40 UTC), with `tools/hot-expert/v1_step2a_kl.sh`
computing the KL **outside the lock** afterwards. Logs `~/bench/v1_step2a.log`,
`~/bench/v1_step2a_kl.log`, `~/bench/v1_step2b.log`; data
`~/bench/v1_step2a_out/`, `~/bench/v1_step2b_out/`. One binary throughout,

#### What the tier holds, and how it says so

```
[qtier-vk] dev3: 0.0 of 25.7 GB used, reserve 1.0 -> budget 24.72 GB (~13968 experts at 1.69 MB each)
[qtier-vk] planned 10240 experts (18.12 GB of a 24.72 GB budget)
[qtier]    warmstart (parallel): all 10240 experts in RAM, 10240 in VRAM -- 6.9 s
[qtier-vk] resident 10240/10240 experts | uploads 10240 | refused 0 | budget-stop 0
[qtier-vk] dev3 planned 18.12 GB, driver reports 18.26 of 25.72 GB used
[qtier-vk] VRAM hit rate: 100.0 % (hits 202240, CPU misses 0)
```

The whole expert set fits on one card with room to spare — the plan estimated
~20 GB, the measurement is 18.12 GB of payload — and the fill takes **6.9–7.0 s**.
`COLI_VK_EXPERTS3` was not needed and was left unset; the 1.0 GB reserve never
fired.

**V1-STEP0 §(f)'s open question about `dev_alloc_footprint` is answered by
measurement: the cudaMalloc granularity curve does NOT transfer, and porting it
would have been wrong.** Payload accounting predicted 18.12 GB and the driver
reports **18.26 GB** — a **0.8 %** gap, against the **22–28 %** CUDA's
allocator costs (`qwen36_tier.c:564`). `backend_vulkan.c` suballocates from
256 MB arena blocks, so per-tensor rounding is `req.alignment`, not a
megabyte-scale quantum. The live `coli_vk_mem_budget3` check stays as the
runaway guard it was ported to be (G6's rule), and it never had to act.

#### Numerics: a per-position KL oracle on the 564-token packet

Reference = the same binary with `Q36_VULKAN` unset (step 1 proved that arm
bit-identical to `qwen36`). `kl_compare.py` unchanged, reading `qwen36` dumps
through the `Q36_LOGIT_DUMP_ALL` container step 1 added.

| pair | positions | mean KL | max KL (position) | top-1 agree | last-pos cosine | maxabs |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| **V1 tier-on vs tier-off, ladder packet** | 625 | **−1.20e-10** | 2.75e-08 (482) | **100.00 %** (625/625) | **1.000000000** | 9.30e-06 |
| **V1 tier-on vs tier-off, short prompt** | 22 | **2.71e-09** | 2.36e-08 (3) | **100.00 %** (22/22) | **1.000000000** | 6.20e-06 |

**The bar applied, stated before the runs** (`v1_step2a_kl.sh`'s header):
mean KL < 0.0284 **and** top-1 ≥ 99.0 % — strictly better than the mildest
defect this record carries. §X2's rows are the scale: G15's rejected int3
experts 0.251 / 78.01 %, G14's rejected int8 kernel 0.0296 / 93.44 %, the
swiglu-clamp gap 0.0284 / 92.73 %. V1 comes in **seven to nine orders of
magnitude below the bar**, which is what the transformation predicts: the same
packed int4 weights (bit-exact through the staging XOR,
`test_qwen36_vk_nibble`), the same gs64 group scales applied per group on both
sides, re-associated — AVX2 lanes per group on the CPU, `subgroupAdd` across
lanes on the GPU — plus the one ordering change `qwen36.c`'s `moe()` makes on
its own account (with the tier on it computes the SHARED expert per token
inside the routed loop so it overlaps the GPU group, instead of once per chunk
in `qwen_shared_experts_cpu`).

**The packet's mean KL is reported as −1.20e-10 and that minus sign is the
oracle's floor, not a negative divergence.** `kl_compare` forms KL as a
difference of logsumexp terms; at 1e-10 against logits of order 10 the result
is float64 cancellation noise. The honest reading is that both dumps are the
same to the last bits the oracle can resolve, which the 100 % top-1 agreement
and the 1.000000000 cosine say without a sign.

`teacher_forcing` (625 and 22 positions) and greedy text are **IDENTICAL** on
both prompts, tier-on against tier-off — an argmax-level agreement the KL then
quantifies. The tier is silent in both tier-off runs, as a tier-off run must be.

#### Multi-request identity: `qwen36` has no KV slots, and what was checked instead

`tworeq.py`'s four-slot check does not apply to this engine. `c/qwen36.c`'s
`serve_read_req` parses the SUBMIT line's slot field and discards it
(`(void)slot`), `serve_loop` reads and serves exactly one request at a time,
and `serve_one` resets the recurrent state, `kv_len`, `first_step`, the
resident set and the router EMA on **every** request. There is no slot state to
collide and no cross-request prefix reuse.

What was run instead, on the tier-on arm, is the invariant that does exist and
is where a tier bug would land: **P1, then P2, then P1 again in one server
process.** The two P1 replies are **IDENTICAL** (60 non-space characters,
coherent text), so nothing leaks across requests through the tier's
issue/take state.

#### What this does and does not say

V1 moves the **routed experts** and nothing else. The DeltaNet recurrence, the
attention, the dense projections, the LM head and the shared expert are all
still on the CPU — `qt_place_of` returns CPU here by design (the R4 trunk
placement was not ported). So 21.6 tok/s is a CPU-bound token with the expert
bucket removed, not a resident-model number, and the remaining ~46 ms/token has
not been profiled. **The plan's withdrawn "≤ 28 tok/s" figure brackets this
result from above, but not for its stated reason:** that derivation assumed
≥ 3 submits per layer; a decode token here is **one** `qt_issue`/`qt_take` pair
per layer, 40 submits, ~1.0 ms/token of driver submit at §X1's measured ~25 µs
— about 2 % of the token. Where the other 98 % goes is the next question on
this engine, not this item's.

Not verified: any depth beyond 459 tokens, any concurrency (the engine has
none), prefix reuse across turns (`qwen36` has no checkpointing; the ladder
reports `REUSE UNVERIFIED (http)` on every turn and both arms re-prefill in
full), and H2b's engine-vs-engine comparison, which is a separate item.

## X3 step 0 (2026-09-16): which bucket grows from 2.5k to 18k — **NOT MEASURABLE from the H2 A-arm logs, and the reason is a defect in the instrument, not in the run.** The ≥ 30 % test is undecided; the prior points at the DSA indexer hard enough to be worth one window, so X3 is **not dead at step 0**

The plan's §4 X3 row and §7 both say this step costs no extra rig time: read
`[OPTIME] mla split` out of the H2 chain's A-arm engine log. That is not
possible, and the reason is worth more than the step was.

### The A-arm logs carry no `[OPTIME]` line, and no engine-mode log ever can

`~/bench/ctx_ladder_out/fk09161755_A1_engine.log` and `_A2_engine.log` are
**30 lines each**: the `[MAP]` and `[VK]` banner, the expert-budget lines,
`[stop]`, `KV_SLOTS`, `slot KV`, two `cache:` lines and `REUSE 1`–`REUSE 8`.
Nothing else. `grep -l OPTIME ~/bench/ctx_ladder_out/*` returns nothing at
all — not for this tag, not for any earlier ladder tag.

The knob was **not** the omission. `franken_chain.sh` `run_A()` exports
`COLI_TIMERS=1`, with a comment naming this very step. The table still cannot
appear, for a reason that lives in the shutdown path:

1. `c/glm53.c`: the table is printed by `optime_print()`, declared
   `__attribute__((destructor))`. A GCC destructor runs when `main()` returns
   (or on `exit()`), and at no other time.
2. Under `SERVE=1` the only way to that return is `serve_loop()` leaving its
   `for (;;)`, which happens on one condition —
   `if (!serve_read_req(&q, verb, sizeof(verb))) break;   /* EOF: si esce */`
   — i.e. **stdin EOF**. Then `main()` does `serve_loop(...); return 0;`.
3. `glm53` installs no signal handler: there is no `signal(`, `sigaction`,
   `SIGTERM` or `SIGINT` anywhere in `c/glm53.c`.
4. The harness never sends that EOF. `ttft_serve.EngineDriver.close()` calls
   `openai_server.Engine.close()`, which does `self.process.terminate()` —
   SIGTERM — then `kill()` after a 5 s grace.

SIGTERM's default disposition terminates the process without running
`atexit`/destructors. **So the `[OPTIME]` table has been silently discarded on
every engine-mode run this harness has ever made**, and `COLI_TIMERS=1` in
engine mode buys the timers' overhead and returns nothing.

Why no gate caught it: **every `[OPTIME]` table in this file comes from the
CLI** (`--greedy`, `profile_run.sh`, `prefill_profile.sh`, the Q-track
chains), which returns from `main()` normally. No chain has ever parsed an
`[OPTIME]` line out of an engine-mode log, so nothing was ever there to be
seen missing. This is the same shape as P7b and the 256-token cap: the
instrument was believed, not checked.

### What the H2 A arms do measure — the quantity step 0 has to attribute

Whole-token decode time from each turn's `decode_tps` in the jsonl
(`(n−1)/(done−first)` over that turn's generation). Both A arms, same chain,
same binary, same corpus — a repeat of the headline, not a paired A/B:

| turn | ctx (prompt tokens) | gen | A1 ms/token | A2 ms/token |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 1 | 1 287 | 128 | 209.5 | 208.5 |
| 2 | 2 655 | 128 | 235.2 | 235.5 |
| 3 | 5 112 | 128 | 290.0 | 267.1 |
| 4 | 9 459 | 128 | 329.5 | 328.7 |
| 5 | **18 439** | 128 | **440.7** | **440.3** |
| 6 (follow-up) | 18 586 | 89 | 452.6 | 452.5 |
| 7 (follow-up) | 18 694 | 68 | 445.6 | 447.0 |

Growth from ~2.5k to ~18.4k: **+205.5 ms/token (A1)** and **+204.8 (A2)**,
i.e. **+87 %** on both arms, agreeing to 0.4 ms at each end. Turn 3 is the
only row where the arms separate (23 ms); every other row is within 1.5 ms.

That +205 ms/token is exactly the number X3 step 0 exists to attribute. These
rows **partition nothing** — they are one wall-clock figure per turn.

### The ≥ 30 % test

**Undecided. The share of attention+indexer at 18k is not measurable from
these logs, because the per-bucket split was never written to them.**

### What this record already implies — a prediction, explicitly NOT a verdict

From §"Long context: the indexer is real…", §G5 and §RP1's correction, all
already measured here and not re-derived:

- `index` is exactly linear per call, and after G5 the per-context-token
  constant is **0.78 µs** at ctx≈786 and **0.87 µs** at ctx≈1 514; 11 DSA
  layers per token.
- `attn` ≈ 1.44 ms + 28.07 µs × min(ctx, 2051) per call — **flat above 2 051
  by construction**, because `coli_sparse_index_width()` returns
  `topk + pool − 1` = 2051 and the attention loop runs over that width.
- `proj` is flat in context.

Taking 0.83 µs: the indexer is ≈ **24 ms/token at ctx 2 655** and ≈ **168
ms/token at ctx 18 439** — Δ ≈ **+144** of the measured **+205**, and
168/441 = **≈ 38 % of the 18k token from the indexer alone**, before the
attention core is counted at all. On its face that clears the ≥ 30 % bar.

**Three reasons that is not allowed to stand as the verdict:**

1. The fit's two points sit at ctx 786 and 1 514, **both below the 2 051
   cap**. §"Long context" states its own caveat plainly: the flattening above
   the cap is derived from the code, not measured, and "if `attn` does *not*
   flatten near 2k, this whole ranking inverts". 18 439 is 9× the cap and no
   measurement in this file has ever been taken above it.
2. The `attn` figure those crossovers use — 211 ms/token (649/3.08, §RP1's
   correction of §G8) — predates G11, G14, G15 and the whole Q track.
   168 + 211 = 379 against a measured 441 ms token would leave ~62 ms for the
   KDA layers, the dense FFN, the MoE bucket, hc+norm and the head combined,
   which is not credible; so at least one of those stale numbers is wrong.
   Choosing which, here, would be the third guess §G5 already warned this
   file against.
3. It says nothing about **KV read bandwidth**, which is X3's stated kill
   condition. The latent cache is 33.0 KB per token across 11 DSA layers
   (this run's own `cache:` line), so a token at depth 18 439 has ~608 MB of
   KV behind it; the DSA path is supposed to touch only 2 051 selected
   entries of it, but the *indexer's* pooled-key sweep is O(ctx) and its
   traffic has never been separated from its arithmetic on this engine. §Q14
   measured a 21–23 % loss of achieved DRAM bandwidth on loops that did not
   change, so "it is the indexer" and "it is memory" are not exclusive here.

**Verdict: X3 is not dead at step 0, and it is not alive either.** The prior
points hard enough at the indexer to justify the window; it does not replace
it.

### What a later lock window must run

**Not engine mode** — that is the finding above. `--greedy` is the only path
that prints the table, and it is the path every `[OPTIME]` row in this file
came from. Two runs, shallow then deep, in a chain script under
`run_chain.sh` so the lock is taken and the gateway is stopped and restored
on every exit path:

```bash
#!/bin/bash
# x3_step0_chain.sh — the decode-phase [OPTIME] split at two depths.
# Launch ONLY as:
#   setsid nohup ~/src/colibri/tools/hot-expert/run_chain.sh \
#       ~/bench/x3_step0_chain.sh > ~/bench/x3_step0.log 2>&1 < /dev/null &
set -u
M=$HOME/models/GLM-5.3-Flash-colibri-int4-g64
BIN=$HOME/bench/glm53.devmerge          # the binary in service; any pristine works
OUT=$HOME/bench/x3_step0; mkdir -p "$OUT"

# The ladder's corpus IS this record file (ttft_serve.DEFAULT_TEXT), so pin it
# to the revision the H2 chain ran against or the depths drift as the record
# grows:
CORPUS=$OUT/corpus.md
( cd "$HOME/src/colibri" && git show 32a46af:tools/hot-expert/ROME-3x7900XTX-2026-09-04.md ) > "$CORPUS"
Q=$'\n\nContinue summarising the notes above in a few sentences, without repeating what you already said.'
head -c  9000 "$CORPUS" > "$OUT/p_shallow.txt"; printf '%s' "$Q" >> "$OUT/p_shallow.txt"
head -c 62000 "$CORPUS" > "$OUT/p_deep.txt";    printf '%s' "$Q" >> "$OUT/p_deep.txt"

pkill -f "openai_[s]erver.py"; sleep 3; pkill -9 -x glm53 2>/dev/null
while pgrep -x glm53 >/dev/null; do sleep 2; done

export OMP_NUM_THREADS=8 OMP_PLACES=cores OMP_PROC_BIND=close
export COLI_VULKAN=1 COLI_VK_DEV2=auto COLI_VK_DEV3=auto
export COLI_VK_SHADERS="$HOME/src/colibri/c/shaders"
export COLI_VK_EXPERTS2=1695 COLI_VK_EXPERTS3=1695
export COLI_KDA_GPU=2
export COLI_TIMERS=1 GLM53_VERBOSE=1
export GLM53_PREFIX_CKPT=0
export COLI_CKPT_DIR="$OUT/ckpt"; mkdir -p "$COLI_CKPT_DIR"
# Freeze the histogram: COLI_USAGE_PATH is rewritten at exit, so the canonical
# file must not be the one the runs mutate (profile_run.sh's rule).
cp "$HOME/.glm53_explain.bin" "$OUT/hist.bin"; export COLI_USAGE_PATH="$OUT/hist.bin"

warm() { find "$M" -type f -name '*.safetensors' -print0 \
         | while IFS= read -r -d '' f; do cat "$f" >/dev/null; done; }

leg() {   # leg <tag> <prompt-file>
  warm
  fincore --bytes --output FILE,SIZE,RES "$M"/*.safetensors | tail -n +2 \
    | awk -v tag="$1" '{t+=int(($2+4095)/4096)*4096; r+=$3} END{printf "[resid %s] %.4f%%\n",tag,100*r/t}'
  echo "### ===== $1 ====="
  # Positional 512 = expert-cache slots/layer, what the serve harness uses.
  # Without it the CLI sizes the cache from MemAvailable and evicts the model
  # under itself (prefill_profile.sh's lesson).
  "$BIN" --model "$M" --prompt "$(cat "$2")" --greedy 32 512 2>&1 \
    | grep -E '^\[OPTIME\]|^\[PROF\]|caricamento|^teacher_forcing' | cut -c1-240
  while pgrep -x glm53 >/dev/null; do sleep 2; done
}

leg shallow "$OUT/p_shallow.txt"
leg deep    "$OUT/p_deep.txt"
echo "### done"
```

The row to read is
`[OPTIME] mla split (n=…, mean ctx=…): proj=… index=… attn=… | index/ctx=… us`
— it prints its own `mean ctx`, so the depth each leg actually reached is
recorded by the run rather than assumed from the char count. `optime_reset()`
fires immediately before the `--greedy` loop, so every figure is
**decode-only**, comparable to §G3/§G5/§RP1–3. `attention+indexer` for the
≥ 30 % test is `(proj + index + attn) × 11` against the `layers`+`head` total
of the same table.

**Cost, honestly: this is not a 30-minute window.** The deep leg pays a cold
18.4k prefill, which this file's own derived figure puts at **≈ 69 min**,
plus ~7 min of load and the warms; the shallow leg is ~13 min. Budget
**≈ 1 h 45 m of rig lock**, and run it overnight.

### The cheaper route, which is also the fix

Give the engine a clean EOF instead of a SIGTERM and the *next* ladder A arm
carries this table for free, at zero extra rig time — which is what the plan
assumed it already had. In `ttft_serve.EngineDriver.close()`, close the
engine's stdin and wait before falling back to `Engine.close()`:
`self.eng.process.stdin.close()`, then `self.eng.process.wait(timeout=60)`,
then the existing body unchanged as the fallback.  Harness-only, no engine
rebuild, no numerics.

**Not applied here**, and deliberately: it must not go into
`openai_server.Engine.close()` (that is the owner's gateway shutdown path),
and closing stdin underneath the dispatcher thread needs one run on the rig
to prove it does not raise where `_fail_pending` would otherwise have run.
The rig lock was held by a hipEngine chain for the whole of this step, so
nothing was run. It is a ten-line change with a five-minute smoke test, and
it is worth doing before the next ladder rather than after.

**What the table format gives, and what it does not.** Each `[OPTIME
req=N ctx=C]` table gives, per bucket, total seconds, a call count `n`, and
therefore ms/call — `optime_reset()` now fires once at the START of
`serve_one()` (matching the CLI path's own reset-before-the-window-it-
measures order, used there to make the destructor's table decode-only), so
this window covers the WHOLE request: prefill chunks AND decode steps
together, not decode-only as every other `[OPTIME]` row in this file is.
`forwards=N` is therefore prefill-forward-calls plus decode-steps, not
tokens-generated, and no `ms/token` figure can be pulled out of this
data without first splitting prefill from decode — the format gives
ms/call, not ms/token, and that is what is copied below rather than
mislabelled. Separating prefill from decode within a request is future
work, not this step's.

**Step 0 verdict (Fable, 2026-09-17 20:10 UTC) — the ≥ 30 % test PASSES; the DSA indexer is the depth term.** Read from the per-request tables above, engine log `~/bench/ctx_ladder_out/f409171830_F4_engine.log`. The ladder-turn windows (req 2–6) are prefill-dominated (turn 6 at 18.4k: 197 forwards for a 8.9k-token prefill plus 128 decode tokens) and say nothing about decode. The two follow-up windows (req 7 and 8, ctx 18 586 / 18 693: a ~147-token follow-up prompt in ~25 forwards plus 64 decode tokens, 89 and 92 forwards) are the decode-shaped ones, and both read the same to three digits:

| bucket at ~18.6k (req 7) | total | per forward (÷ 89) | share of the 509 ms forward |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| mla: index (DSA indexer) | 24.453 s | **275 ms** | **54 %** |
| mla: attn core | 3.77 s | 42 ms | 8 % |
| mla: proj | 0.756 s | 8.5 ms | 2 % |
| kda (34 linear-attention layers) | 3.754 s | 42 ms | 8 % |
| ffn_moe (router + shared + experts, GPU and CPU) | 11.106 s | 125 ms | 25 % |
| ffn_dense | 0.382 s | 4.3 ms | 1 % |
| hc+norm | 1.055 s | 12 ms | 2 % |

Per MLA call the indexer costs 25.0 ms at ctx 18 630 (24.453 s / 979 calls; 11 MLA layers per forward); at ctx 1 304 (req 2) it was 5.81 ms/call, `index/ctx = 4.46 µs` per context token per call. **Caveat, stated:** the 25 prefill forwards in each follow-up window carry ~6 rows each; if the indexer's cost were linear in rows, the decode-only share would be as low as 24.45 s / (25·6 + 64) ≈ 114 ms/token = 26 %; if it is bandwidth-bound on the pooled-key read (the G5 cache, which is what the `index/ctx` slope measures), rows are nearly free and the per-forward 275 ms stands (54 %). The record's own post-G5 slope predicted ~168 ms/token at 18.4k (38 %, above). Three estimates, all ≥ 26 % and two ≥ 38 %: **the indexer is the growing bucket, attention core + indexer together are 34–62 % of the 18k token, and X3 (a stricter, cheaper selection at depth, knob-gated under X2's bar) is the decode item for GLM-5.3-Flash.** A decode-only window (the two-depth CLI chain in this section, or one ladder follow-up with a 1-token prompt and `--gen 256`) pins the share; it is not needed for the decision. **Ceiling, so nobody over-promises:** holding the indexer at its 1.3k cost (64 ms/forward) makes the 18k token ≈ 300 ms → ≈ 3.3 tok/s; removing it altogether ≈ 234 ms → ≈ 4.3 tok/s. Decode on this model at 18k does not reach 5 tok/s through X3 alone; the next ms after that are the MoE bucket (125 ms/forward here, of which the CPU misses are ≤ 45 ms) and the KDA layers (42 ms). Oracle for this run: `teacher_forcing` IDENTICAL, candidate vs served pristine, timers off (chain `f409171830`, accept_live PASS).

17:55:31 UTC, expected end ~22:00 UTC, confirmed still running via

no lock was taken, no GPU was touched, and the smoke/ladder run (phase 2)

**hipEngine, from its own docs (`~/src/hipEngine` on the rig, README.md,
docs/ENVS.md, docs/API.md, docs/KERNELS.md, docs/GGUF.md), current release
v0.5.0, AGPL-3.0-or-later:**

- **ROCm support:** "ROCm 7.x is the safest choice for the current wheel
  (ROCm 10.0 has been tested and works fine as well)" — this box's
  `~/venvs/rocm` (TheRock stable wheels, ROCm 10.0.0, gfx1100 device pack,
  Python 3.14.4, already built for arm B per FRANKEN-H0d) is an explicitly
  supported combination, reused unchanged rather than a second venv.
- **How it finds HIP:** requires `hipcc` and `libamdhip64.so` on the
  platform; no dedicated hipEngine-only discovery env var beyond the normal
  ROCm ones. Device selection is `HIP_VISIBLE_DEVICES` (docs/ENVS.md) /
  `ROCR_VISIBLE_DEVICES` — "do not stack `HIP_VISIBLE_DEVICES=1` and
  `ROCR_VISIBLE_DEVICES=1` unless that is intentional." No hipFire-style
  `HIPFIRE_DEVICES` name exists; `--backend hip_gfx1100` /
  `HIPENGINE_BACKEND` forces the target only when auto-detection needs help
  (this box's card auto-detects as `gfx1100`, so left on auto).
- **Install:** `pip install hipengine huggingface_hub` from PyPI, or a
  source checkout with `git lfs pull` + `pip install -e .`. Chosen: the
  source checkout (`~/src/hipEngine`, shallow clone), because the AOTriton
  gfx1100 attention runtime (`hipengine/kernels/hip_gfx1100/attention/aotriton_runtime/`,
  `.so`/`.aks2` blobs, 17 MB `libaotriton_v2.so.0.11.2` plus per-shape
  `.aks2` images) is LFS-tracked and the editable install is what the plan
  asked for. **The rig has no `git-lfs` and no sudo; `~/bin` is root-owned
  (`drwxr-xr-x root root`), not user-writable.** Fetched the `git-lfs`
  v3.5.1 linux-amd64 static binary from its GitHub release tarball straight
  into `~/.local/bin` (no sudo, nothing outside `$HOME`), `git lfs install
  --local` + `git lfs pull` in the checkout — clean, all AOTriton blobs
  present. `~/venvs/rocm/bin/pip install -e ".[chat]"` then installed
  hipengine 0.5.0 plus fastapi/uvicorn/pydantic/tokenizers/rich/
  prompt_toolkit/etc., **zero native compiles** (every dependency had a
  `cp314` manylinux wheel; hipEngine's own package is pure Python at
  install time). `hipengine --help` / `hipengine serve --help` both run
  clean from `~/venvs/rocm/bin/hipengine`.
- **Serve command / port:** `hipengine serve --model <path-or-repo-id>
  --served-model-name <name> --host <h> --port <p>` (default
  `127.0.0.1:8000`); OpenAI-compatible `/v1/chat/completions` (streaming
  SSE and non-streaming), `/v1/models`, plus a `/v1/hipengine/capabilities`
  extension endpoint reporting the resolved backend/quant/execution-profile,
  MTP/speculative status, and prefix-cache/KV posture after load.
- **JIT-compiles kernels: YES, at first model load.** README: "The first
  model load compiles and caches kernels, so it takes longer than later
  starts." docs/KERNELS.md is explicit: `hipengine.core.build` "calls
  `hipcc` or `nvcc`, links a shared object, loads it with `ctypes.CDLL`, and
  caches by source/flags/compiler/target metadata under
  `~/.cache/hipengine/build/`. It does not use `torch.utils.cpp_extension`."
  This means **the exact same box trap that gated arm B applies here
  unchanged**: this box's clang autodetects the newest, headerless GCC 16
  (no `libstdc++-16-dev`) unless steered off it, so `h2c_chain.sh` exports
  the identical `CPLUS_INCLUDE_PATH=/usr/include/c++/15:/usr/include/x86_64-linux-gnu/c++/15`
  plus `ROCM_PATH`/`HIP_PATH`/`LD_LIBRARY_PATH` pointed at `~/venvs/rocm`'s
  root, verbatim from `run_B` in `franken_chain.sh` / `h0d2_chain.sh`. Not
  yet exercised end-to-end (that is phase 2, i.e. a real model load), so
  this is the documented+reasoned expectation, not yet a measured pass.
- **Model format for Qwen3.6-35B-A3B:** GGUF (`Q4_K_M`, `Q4_K_S`,
  `UD-Q3_K_M`, `UD-Q4_K_M` all listed as tested on `gfx1100`), or hipEngine's
  own ParoQuant W4 packed checkpoint
  (`shisa-ai/Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-PARO-packed`). Chosen: GGUF `UD-Q4_K_M` from
  `unsloth/Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-MTP-GGUF` — the same repo arm B's own MTP sidecar
  comes from (docs/MTP-gguf.md), the file docs/GGUF.md's own "public
  bring-up" fixture and docs/TUNING-gfx1151.md's benchmark both name, and
  the format the README's GGUF-or-ParoQuant section recommends by default
  ("GGUF is now extensively optimized... broader compatibility").
- **Prefix/KV-cache reuse:** `--prefix-cache {off,radix}` server flag,
  **default `off`.** `h2c_chain.sh` passes `radix` explicitly so the
  second, identical 64-token request actually exercises reuse instead of
  measuring an engine started with it disabled. `--kv-storage` defaults to
  `int8_per_token_head` (fails closed to `bf16` on an unqualified artifact).

## §PCIE-STREAM (2026-09-16): host->device streaming bandwidth, 1/2/3 cards concurrent, vs X6's derivation

X6 (`FRANKEN-ENGINE-PLAN-2026-09-15.md` §4) rejected streaming cold GLM
routed experts into the GPU on a *derivation*, not a measurement: one card
at a practical ~25 GB/s (of 32 nominal, itself not measured) against the
CPU int4 path's measured 21.95 GB/s (§G11 above), concluding a per-token
stream loses at batch 1 and nothing amortises because the miss set changes
every token. That derivation covered one card. Three cards pulling
*different* data concurrently is a different sum, and this item measures
it: `tools/hot-expert/pcie_stream_probe.cpp` (HIP, one host thread + one
`hipStream` per device, a start barrier so a multi-device trial is
genuinely concurrent for its whole timed window), driven by
`tools/hot-expert/pcie_stream_chain.sh` through `run_chain.sh` (rig lock
only -- this chain does not stop the gateway, see its own header). Chain
`pcie_09162130`, rc=0, `accept_live`/in-service check by `run_chain.sh`
passed (gateway was never stopped). Full output:
`~/bench/pcie_out/pcie_09162130.txt`, chain log `~/bench/pcie_stream.log`.

**Build note for the next session:** a plain host-linked hipcc build on
this box needs `--gcc-install-dir=/usr/lib/gcc/x86_64-linux-gnu/15`, not
`CPLUS_INCLUDE_PATH` alone -- the latter (h0d_chain.sh's JIT/device-only-build
recipe) compiles the object fine but leaves the link step unable to find
`-lstdc++` (`ld.lld: error: unable to find library -lstdc++`); confirmed
building this probe, same fix as `rocm_p2p_probe.cpp` already used.

**What it says vs X6's assumption, numbers only:**

- One card alone: pinned 14 MiB ~27.98-27.98 GB/s (median 27.98), pageable
  14 MiB ~27.69-27.72 GB/s, pinned 256 MiB ~28.46-28.47 GB/s -- all three
  devices agree within 0.03 GB/s of each other at cfg=1. X6's derivation
  assumed "a practical ~25 GB/s (of 32 nominal, not measured)"; the
  measured one-card figure is 28.0-28.5 GB/s, higher than that assumption
  across every (mem,block) combination measured.
- Two cards concurrent (dev0 `0000:83:00.0` + dev3 `0000:86:00.0`): each
  device drops to ~17.8-18.1 GB/s (from ~28 GB/s alone) while the aggregate
  is 35.7-36.1 GB/s -- roughly 1.28x one card, not 2x, i.e. dev0 and dev3
  share an upstream link and do not sum linearly.
- Three cards concurrent: dev2 (`0000:48:00.0`) keeps ~27.66-28.47 GB/s
  (its cfg=1 rate, unchanged), while dev0 and dev3 drop further to
  ~16.6-16.8 GB/s each (summing to ~33.3-33.5 GB/s between the two of
  them); the three-card aggregate is 60.8-62.0 GB/s across the three
  (mem,block) combinations.
- Against the CPU int4 expert kernel's measured 21.95 GB/s (§G11): the
  three-card aggregate (60.8-62.0 GB/s) is 2.77-2.82x that byte rate; the
  one-card figure alone (28.0-28.5 GB/s) is already 1.28-1.30x it.
- The 8-thread CPU DRAM-read control (14 MiB blocks out of a 4 GiB buffer,
  same OMP env as the recorded 8-thread numbers) measured 91.629 GB/s --
  not the same figure as the CPU int4 kernel's 21.95 GB/s (that number is
  the achieved rate of the actual quantized-decode kernel, ~27% of DRAM
  bandwidth per §G11's own accounting; this is a raw summation loop's
  ceiling on the same box, order-of-magnitude consistent with the ~81 GB/s
  that accounting implies).

**Correction to the reuse reading (Fable, 2026-09-16 22:40 UTC), applies to this section and to §FRANKEN-H2's hipFire rows.** The r = T_lad/T_cold rule in plan §2.4 assumed T_lad measures a follow-up at the same depth. It does not: the ladder's T_lad at "16k" is turn 5's TTFT, and turn 5 prefills the new ~8.9k-token step on top of a 9.5k prefix. With reuse working, r is therefore the new-token fraction (8 891/18 372 = 0.48), and the measured r of 0.53–0.56 for RV/RH and 0.48 for OV18/OV36 is what a reusing server produces; without reuse r would be ≈ 1. The direct evidence is the follow-up rows: turn 6 adds ~150 tokens at 18.5k depth and answers in 0.646–0.681 s (RV), 0.659–0.661 s (RH), 3.63–3.66 s (OV18), 6.30–6.32 s (OV36) against 14.05–14.25 s (RV), 7.76–7.79 s (RH), 137 s (OV18), 244 s (OV36) for a cold prefill of that depth. llama.cpp reuses the prefix on every arm. The same reading applied to §FRANKEN-H2: hipFire's follow-ups at 85k depth took 2.345/0.436 s (B1) and 2.347/0.440 s (B2) against 53.2 s for its own turn 11 prefill; hipFire reuses too, and Q2's "NO VERDICT" there is the rule's artefact, not the engine's. The r thresholds are withdrawn; the follow-up TTFT at depth is the reuse number from here on (plan rev 11).

No call returned REFUSED (2); this is `context_compare.py`'s own documented "accepted outcome" (the chain prints `REFUSED/NO VERDICT is an accepted outcome` after every compare call), not a script failure. **The r-rule itself is withdrawn (FRANKEN-ENGINE-PLAN-2026-09-15.md, Rev 11, 2026-09-16 22:45 UTC), not just these readings.** A ladder step labelled "16k" (or any depth here) prefills only the NEW tokens since the previous step -- for GF's own 8192->16384 step that is ~9-10k new tokens against a much larger already-cached prefix -- so a genuinely reusing server reads r ≈ 0.5 by construction; that is exactly what GF1 and GF2 read at every depth above the shallowest sweep point (0.466-0.632 above), the same pattern rev 11 found on every other arm it checked (llama.cpp's gpt-oss arms in record §GPTOSS-3CARD, hipFire in §FRANKEN-H2). **The follow-up TTFT at depth is the reuse evidence instead**: turns 6-7 above are a ~130-150 token new question against an already-18.3-18.5k-token context, and GF answers it in 5.5-7.1 s (GF1: 7.121s / 5.566s; GF2: 7.117s / 5.542s) rather than paying anything close to the 52-108 s a same-sized NEW-content ladder step costs at that depth -- GF reuses, by the same standard record §FRANKEN-H2 and §GPTOSS-3CARD apply to hipFire (0.3-0.7s at 18.5k) and llama.cpp's gpt-oss arms.

Not a controlled A/B, but a real, unplanned demonstration of the header note's own page-cache claim: the second fresh process load is ~10x faster with nothing changed but what was already in RAM.

**Residency at chain end.** `warm_glm` (the exit trap's re-warm of Colibri's own 182 GiB GLM_SNAP) settled at 68.08% resident (`[resid final] resident=68.0827%`, below the 90% floor the chain warns on) at restart time, before `accept_live.sh`'s own requests ran and presumably pulled in more of the working set -- `accept_live.sh` itself PASSED regardless (ttft 9.47s / 7.24s on its two new-chat checks). Consistent with the header's own page-cache note: the 149 GB GF model evicted more of Colibri's 182 GiB shards than one `cat` pass alone restored before the gateway came back up.

**What this says (numbers only, both arms agree within ~4% of each other).** GF (llama.cpp, UD-IQ4_XS, CPU offload, -ngl 18) decodes SLOWER than A (Colibri) at shallow depth (turn 1: -39.9% conservative; turn 4: -8.0% conservative) and FASTER at deep context (turn 5: +23.0%; turn 7: +26.4% conservative) -- the two curves cross between turn 4 (9.3-9.5k tokens) and turn 5 (18.3-18.4k tokens). Follow-up TTFT at ~18.4-18.7k is within ±4-16% either way (turn 6: GF +3.7% slower conservative; turn 7: GF -16.0% faster conservative). Cold TTFT at full ladder depth (~18.3k, derived = sum of step prefills) is 237-238s for GF against 2561/2558s for A -- GF's cold prefill at this depth is roughly 10.8x faster. Reuse ratio is NO VERDICT by the withdrawn r-rule at every depth on both arms; the follow-up-TTFT evidence above says GF reuses. This entry does not recommend which deployment to serve (that decision, same as record §FRANKEN-H2's own closing line, belongs to the plan owner, not this table) -- GF's shallow-depth decode floor (~2.7-2.9 tok/s) is close to A's OWN deep-depth floor (~2.2-2.3 tok/s), so a workload's context-depth distribution decides more than either arm's headline number does.

FRANKEN-ENGINE-PLAN-2026-09-15.md §8.3 item F0: §PCIE-STREAM measured

HIP, so F2's projected expert-stream rate has to be re-measured on the API
the engine actually uses. `tools/hot-expert/vk_stream_probe.c` (one pthread
per physical device, persistent VkDevice/queue/pool/fence, batch_size=4
copies per `vkCmdCopyBuffer` submit, start barrier for concurrent multi-device
trials, same 1/2/3-card interleave 1,2,3,3,2,1, 14 MiB / 256 MiB blocks, >= 2
s/trial, median of n=6), driven by `tools/hot-expert/vk_stream_chain.sh`
through `run_chain.sh` (rig lock only -- gateway not stopped, per that
chain's own header). Chain tag `vkstream_09172001`, `run_chain vk_stream_chain
exited rc=0 2026-09-17T20:08:15+0000` (queued behind the F4 chain, which held
the lock from 18:30 to ~20:01 UTC; launched by `~/bench/f0_queue.sh` at
20:01:50 UTC). Full output: `~/bench/vk_stream_out/vkstream_09172001.txt`,
chain log `~/bench/vk_stream.log`.

**Bus id -> dev name mapping, verified from `VK_EXT_pci_bus_info`
(`VkPhysicalDevicePCIBusInfoPropertiesEXT`) this run** (matches
§PCIE-STREAM's HIP mapping; enumeration order on Vulkan is dev0, dev2, dev3 --

**ext-host result: unavailable on every device/config.** One reason string
(all instances identical, quoted once, not per-row):
`vkAllocateMemory(import) rc=-13 (EACCES) -- amdgpu userptr rejects any
file-backed VMA (vm_file set), confirmed independent of per-page COW state;
anonymous host memory imports fine`. Isolated by standalone testing
(2026-09-17, not shipped): a `MAP_ANONYMOUS` region imports successfully
(`vkAllocateMemory` rc=0) on the same device via the same
`VK_EXT_external_memory_host` / `HOST_ALLOCATION_BIT_EXT` path; a
`MAP_PRIVATE` mapping of the GLM shard fails with the same rc=-13 even after
every page was dirtied (memset) before import, i.e. after every page had
already copy-on-write'd to anonymous -- the VMA still carries a backing
`vm_file`, and amdgpu's userptr registration rejects that regardless of the
per-page state. A kernel/driver restriction on this rig's amdgpu stack, not
a probe bug; working around it by copying the bytes into anonymous memory
first would just be the memcpy+upload path again.

### F0b (2026-09-17, same day): the transfer-preferred queue family was the bottleneck, not Vulkan itself

Amendment before the F0 gate above was accepted: every row above ran on
this probe's transfer-preferred queue family (`qfam_xfer`, chosen for
`TRANSFER_BIT` without `GRAPHICS_BIT` -- RADV's async-compute/SDMA family).
On RADV that family is known to be far slower than the GPU's own
compute/graphics engines for host->device traffic, so the F0 gate could
not be decided on it alone. `vk_stream_probe.c` gained two more source
kinds on `pick_backend_qfam()`'s family -- the SAME algorithm
`backend_vulkan.c`'s `coli_vk_init()` uses (first family with
`VK_QUEUE_COMPUTE_BIT` set) -- and was rerun, same configs, same chain
(`vkstream_09172024`, `run_chain vk_stream_chain exited rc=0
2026-09-17T20:35:03+0000`, gateway not stopped, back in service after).
Full output: `~/bench/vk_stream_out/vkstream_09172024.txt`.

## §F2-STEP0 (2026-09-18): the staging fill -- CPU fill alone clears the bar, the ring pipeline does not

FRANKEN-ENGINE-PLAN-2026-09-15.md §8.3 item F2, step 0: F0/F0b (record
§VK-STREAM) measured the GPU-side leg of F2's streamed prefill --
`shader-host-read` on the backend's own queue family reaches 62-63 GB/s on
three cards -- but F0's own single-thread memcpy into that staging buffer
managed only 15 GB/s, and F2's chunk arithmetic assumes the fill keeps up.
This step measures the fill multi-threaded, in the scattered (miss-pattern)
access F2 will actually have, and the fill overlapped with the GPU read in
a real ring-buffer pipeline: `tools/hot-expert/staging_fill_probe.c`
(extends `vk_stream_probe.c`'s setup, reuses `vk_stream_reduce.comp`
unmodified via descriptor-offset binding to ring slots), driven by
`tools/hot-expert/f2_step0_chain.sh` through `run_chain.sh` (rig lock only
-- gateway not stopped, same reasoning as `vk_stream_chain.sh`). Built and
run from a fresh clone (`~/src/colibri-f2s0`, branch
`perf/f2-step0-staging-fill`), gateway never stopped. Two full runs, same
chain, same shard set, five minutes apart:

| run | tag | rc | in service after |
|---|---|---:|---|
| 1 | `f2s0_09172251` | 0 | `/v1/models=200`, glm53 sha `a8e10ecf09edc05c` |
| 2 | `f2s0_09172256` | 0 | `/v1/models=200`, glm53 sha `a8e10ecf09edc05c` |

Full output: `~/bench/f2_step0_out/f2s0_09172251.txt`,
`~/bench/f2_step0_out/f2s0_09172256.txt`; chain log `~/bench/f2_step0.log`.
No coincidental gateway request landed during either run (`owui_report.sh
3` before and after both show the same three pre-existing requests). No
WARN line fired in either run (residency did not drop; it rose slightly,
page cache warming further from the reads).

**Machine facts (both runs):**

| | run 1 | run 2 |
|---|---:|---:|
| MemAvailable before (kB) | 238683744 | 238694124 |
| MemAvailable after (kB) | 238658128 | 238662464 |
| residency before (%) | 94.24 | 94.36 |
| residency after (%) | 94.36 | 94.36 |

Shard set: 62 files, 13237 x 14 MiB blocks (194.3 GB), fixed seed 42, 2048
random block offsets. VRAM preflight/postflight on all three cards matched
within noise both runs (card0/card2 ~1.5 GiB free, card1 ~2.5 GiB free,
throughout).

median of n=5 trials each, >= 2 s/trial, GB = 1e9 bytes:**

**What the numbers say, before the gate:**

- **Random vs sequential is free here.** memcpy (scattered, fixed-seed
  random blocks) and memcpy-seq (contiguous blocks) are within noise at
  every thread count (e.g. T=8: 59.343/59.376 vs 59.416/59.422). The shard
  set is ~94% page-cache resident (measured, not assumed); at this
  residency a "miss" still only costs a DRAM read, and DRAM has no seek
  penalty. The random-vs-sequential cost F0's plan asked about is not
  where this box's bottleneck is.
- **pread and memcpy also agree within noise** (T=8: 55.79-55.80 pread vs
  59.34-59.38 memcpy) -- `pread` avoids the mmap fault path but does not
  win on an already-resident file.
- **Fill alone clears the plan's 60 GB/s bar.** T=8 memcpy/memcpy-seq reach
  59.3-59.4 GB/s, T=16 essentially matches (58.5-58.5, no further gain from
  SMT siblings -- this box's DRAM bandwidth, not thread count, is the
  ceiling above T=8). Plain multi-threaded fill into HOST_VISIBLE|
  HOST_COHERENT staging is not the obstacle F0 named it as; it is close
  enough to be within a run's noise of the 60 GB/s line.
- **The ring pipeline is the obstacle, and it is not the fill rate.** One
  card alone, fully dedicated 8-thread fill pool: 23.47-23.71 GB/s
  sustained end-to-end -- well below both the fill-alone rate at T=8
  (59.3+ GB/s) and F0's single-card GPU-read rate (26.6-28.3 GB/s,
  §VK-STREAM). The 4-slot x 64 MiB ring's per-cycle handshake (async
  submit, split a 64 MiB slot into 8 chunk-tasks over a mutex/condvar
  queue, wait for the 8th chunk, bounded `vkWaitForFences`) costs more per
  cycle than either leg's raw bytes/sec would predict; this is the ring
  pipeline's own synchronisation overhead, not a fill-bandwidth or
  GPU-read-bandwidth limit. All three cards concurrently, one shared
  8-thread pool: dev2 (unshared upstream link, matching F0's own
  dev0+dev3-share-a-link finding) holds 18.67-18.68 GB/s alone, while dev0
  and dev3 drop to 9.96-10.02 GB/s each under three-way contention for the
  same 8 physical cores -- the aggregate is 38.61-38.67 GB/s.
- Both runs agree to within 0.2% on every row; the pipeline aggregate in
  particular (38.607 vs 38.666) is reproducible, not noise.

**F2 step 0 gate (plan §8.3, F2 row): pipeline aggregate on three cards >=
60 GB/s PASS; 40-60 GB/s marginal (name the limiting leg); < 40 GB/s the F2
chunk arithmetic is off and is rewritten on the measured number.**

Measured (kind=pipeline threads=8 cards=3 dev=all): 38.607 GB/s (run 1),
38.666 GB/s (run 2), mean 38.637 GB/s.
< 40 GB/s: chunk arithmetic rewritten on the measured number.
123 GB / 38.637 GB/s / 512 = 6.218 ms/token (run 1: 6.222 ms/token; run 2: 6.213 ms/token).
Versus today's CPU path (113.9 ms/token, §8.1): 18.3x.
Versus F2's original projection at the GPU-read-only rate (3.9 ms/token, §8.3 F2 row): 1.6x worse.

FRANKEN-ENGINE-PLAN-2026-09-15.md §8.3 item F2, step 0b (coordinator

GB/s ceiling, and does it go away if the copy goes away? §VK-STREAM found
`VK_EXT_external_memory_host` import fails (EACCES) only for file-backed
memory; this step imports ANONYMOUS host memory (populated once from the
shards) and reads it in place with F0's own `shader-host-read` dispatch --
`tools/hot-expert/staging_import_probe.c`, driven by
`tools/hot-expert/f2_step0b_chain.sh` through `run_chain.sh` (rig lock

**Setup facts:** `min_imported_host_ptr_align=4096` on all three devices;
HOST_VISIBLE heap size 123.66 GiB per device (a GTT-style heap, not VRAM);
`/sys/module/amdgpu/parameters/gttsize` is root-only on this rig (read
attempt returned EACCES, reported honestly rather than guessed); THP mode
is `[[madvise]]` (confirmed from `/sys/kernel/mm/transparent_hugepage/
enabled`), so the anon vs anon-huge variants are a genuine A/B, not a

Load-time populate rate (INFO, NOT a gate metric): 7.2-8.6 GB/s for
`anon`, 22.7-33.1 GB/s for `anon-huge` at the sizes that completed.

**The scale trend, three-card aggregate GB/s:**

| size_gib | anon | anon-huge |
|---:|---:|---:|
| 8 | 6.279 | 35.373 |
| 32 | 1.739 | 18.895 |
| 64 | 0.885 | 10.683 |
| 96 | 0.594 | (did not complete) |

Both variants fall sharply and monotonically as the imported region grows
-- `anon-huge` at 8 GiB (35.4 GB/s) is close to §F2-STEP0's pipeline number
(38.6 GB/s), but by 64 GiB it has fallen to 10.7 GB/s, roughly a 3.3x drop
for an 8x size increase. `anon` (4 KiB pages, no THP hint) is an order of
magnitude worse than `anon-huge` at every size and falls just as steeply
(6.3 -> 0.59 GB/s, 8 GiB to 96 GiB). This is consistent with the
scatter-gather cost of a userptr import scaling with the SIZE of the
pinned region (more discontiguous physical pages/SG-list entries to
traverse per access, or per-access lookup cost in the driver's own
tracking structure), not with the 256 MiB window actually read per
dispatch -- i.e. the cost is paid for the WHOLE import's bookkeeping, not
the slice being read, which is the opposite of what F2 needs (F2's
per-chunk working set of non-resident experts, ~123 GB, sits well above
even the 96 GiB point on this curve).

**F2 step 0b gate (coordinator's terms): pipeline aggregate on three cards
>= 50 GB/s AND >= 64 GiB importable -> F2 reads non-resident experts in
place, no staging, no fill; 40-50 marginal; < 40 OR import capped below 64
GiB -> F2 stays on the §F2-STEP0 staging pipeline.**

Importability itself is NOT capped below 64 GiB (96 GiB imported
successfully on all three devices for the `anon` variant). The failure is
bandwidth, and it is not close: best three-card aggregate at 64 GiB is
10.683 GB/s (`anon-huge`), 23x below the 50 GB/s bar, falling further with
scale, not rising. NOT MET. F2 stays on the §F2-STEP0 ring pipeline
(38.637 GB/s mean, 6.22 ms/token for the streamed experts).

**Incident (2026-09-17 -- 2026-09-18, still open at commit time): the 96
GiB `anon-huge` attempt hung and was terminated at the 15-minute rig-time
budget; the underlying kernel thread would not die and is holding the rig
lock.** Sequence: the probe reached `size_gib=96 variant=anon-huge`
(`mmap` + `madvise(MADV_HUGEPAGE)` + populate of a fresh 96 GiB anonymous
region, after the prior `anon` 96 GiB region had already been imported,
read, and freed) and produced no INFO/ROW output for over 12 minutes,
versus 40-90 s for every other combo. Its RSS matched a fully-populated 96
GiB region (`VmRSS` ~96 GiB) and CPU usage had gone to near-zero,
indicating it was blocked rather than working. At the 15-minute mark the
process was sent `SIGTERM` (`pkill -f "staging_import_[p]robe"`, bracket
form per this repo's rig rules). Its main thread became a zombie
immediately, but a second thread of the same (now-defunct) process
remains in **`D` (uninterruptible disk sleep)** state
(`/proc/193104/task/199307`, confirmed unchanged across three checks over
the following 7 minutes) -- almost certainly inside the amdgpu driver,
unpinning/tearing down the large userptr registration for the 96 GiB
import, or a THP-related page operation, interrupted mid-operation by the
signal. A `D`-state thread cannot be killed by any signal, including
`SIGKILL`, and this session has no `sudo`. Consequences at the time this
section was written: **the rig lock (`~/bench/.rig.lock`) remains held by
the stuck chain (`f2_step0b_chain`, pid 193056) and will not release until
that kernel thread completes or the box is rebooted** -- no other chain
can take the lock until then. The gateway itself is UNAFFECTED and
confirmed healthy throughout (`/v1/models` returned 200 at every check
during and after the incident; `MemAvailable` settled at ~139.7 GB, down
from ~238 GB, consistent with the leaked 96 GiB region's pages not yet
being reclaimed, not with any additional loss). This is reported rather
than resolved: clearing a `D`-state kernel thread is outside what a
non-root session can do, and per this fork's own rule a reboot is the
owner's call, not this session's. **A future large-region import/teardown
probe should size its own internal timeout well under any external
deadline (e.g. skip a size once the trend already answers the gate, as
this section's data already does at 64 GiB) rather than relying on being
killed from outside**, precisely because killing it from outside is what
produced this stuck thread.

## F6a (2026-09-19): the DSA indexer's score pass parallelised + exact heap top-512 — gated PASS

Item F6a, `F6-INDEXER-DESIGN-2026-09-18.md` §3(vi) (the recommended design out
of F6). `perf/f6a-index-parallel` sha `bf6afd0` (chain fix `c7d930c`), gated
via `tools/hot-expert/f6a_gate_chain.sh` under `run_chain.sh`. Two chain runs:
tag `f6a09182113` (2026-09-18 21:13–23:03 UTC), which stopped correctly before
the ladder on a chain-side gap, not an engine defect (below); tag
`f6a09182308` (2026-09-18 23:08 UTC – 2026-09-19 00:58 UTC), rc=0. Full logs:
`~/bench/f6a_gate.log`, `~/bench/f6a_out/f6a09182308_*`.

**The change** (`c/sparse_index.h`): the score pass over pools is
`#pragma omp parallel for` (§G7's pattern — disjoint writes, no shared
accumulator, no summation-order change), on two axes chosen per call (rows
for prefill, pools for decode); the O(wanted×pools) greedy top-512 scan
replaced by an exact bounded min-heap + sort, proved equivalent to the
scan's own tie rule. `GLM53_INDEX_SCALAR=1` restores the original scalar
path unchanged; default is the new path.

### Oracle

Run 1 caught a real gap in the CHAIN, not the engine: `teacher_forcing`
**IDENTICAL** at both a 7 495-token deep prompt and a 2 061-token shallow
prompt, the `GLM53_DUMP_INDEX` row dump **IDENTICAL** at both depths (82 445
rows deep, 22 671 rows shallow — set AND rank order), the
`GLM53_INDEX_SCALAR=1` knob-routing check **IDENTICAL** — but the logit-dump
leg came back **REFUSED**: the served pristine (`a8e10ecf09edc05c`) predates
`GLM53_LOGIT_DUMP_ALL` and wrote no dump file at all, so `cmp` had nothing to
compare. The chain correctly stopped before the ladder
(`FATAL: F6a oracle did not come back fully IDENTICAL`), restored the
gateway, and `accept_live.sh` PASSed. Fix (`c7d930c`): since
`teacher_forcing` and the index dump already prove the candidate's
`GLM53_INDEX_SCALAR=1` path is bit-identical to the pristine, the logit-dump
reference became the candidate's OWN scalar-path dump instead of the
(nonexistent) pristine dump — a transitive proof (pristine ≡
candidate-scalar, established two other ways above; candidate-scalar ≡
candidate-default is the new check), not a weakening of the oracle. Run 2
(`F6A_REUSE_ORACLE=1`, reusing run 1's `teacher_forcing`/index-dump outputs
unchanged, re-running only the logit-dump leg against the new reference):
logit dump **BIT-IDENTICAL, 4 643 302 416 bytes** (candidate default vs
candidate `GLM53_INDEX_SCALAR=1`, every prompt position × vocab). What this
does and does not compare: it proves the new parallel/heap path produces
byte-identical logits to the old scalar path on THIS build; it does not
redo the pristine-vs-scalar comparison (that is run 1's `teacher_forcing` +
index-dump legs, both IDENTICAL, unaffected by the fix). All five oracle
legs: **PASS**.

### What this does to F2 (the arithmetic, not a measurement)

F2 replaces the CPU expert path in prefill with streamed experts at a measured
6.22 ms/token (§F2-STEP0b) plus GPU tile compute that has not been measured.
With the streaming cost alone and zero compute, the 18k turn goes 136.4 →
72.8 ms/token: **a ceiling of 1.87× at 18k, 2.4× at depth 0.** The plan's
gate for F2 — "≥ 10× on the 18k ladder-turn TTFT or the item is rejected" —
was written when the prefill token was believed to be 113.9 ms of experts;
rev 15 already withdrew that reading, and this profile puts the number on it:
10× at 18k is 13.6 ms/token, below what attention alone costs today (28.4).
No expert-side item can meet it. After a perfect F2 the 18k token would be
attn 39 %, index 18 %, kda 18 %, streamed experts 9 %, hc 7 %.

## §F2 (2026-09-19): chunked batched prefill with expert streaming — the ring goes in HOST RAM, not VRAM; short ladder 2.02× on turn 1 and 1.80× at 5.1k; the 18k rung is not run here

`FRANKEN-ENGINE-PLAN-2026-09-15.md` §8.3 item **F2**, design note
`tools/hot-expert/F2-STREAM-PREFILL-DESIGN-2026-09-19.md`. Branch
`perf/f2-stream-prefill`, built in `~/src/colibri-f2`; the served binary was
never replaced and nothing was merged. Gate as re-based by plan rev 16: **≥ 1.6×
on the 18k ladder-turn TTFT and ≥ 2.0× on turn 1.** Turn 1 is decided here.
**The 18k rung is NOT run in this section** — it is a multi-hour gateway
outage and is handed back ready to launch.

Knob `COLI_PREFILL_STREAM=1`, off by default, prefill only; decode untouched
(that is F1). With the knob on, the experts the tier does not hold are copied
into a per-device ring and dispatched through the existing
`coli_vk_expert_group_issue/2/3` path instead of going down the CPU int4 path,
and the prefill chunk's effective default rises from 128 to 512.

### Residency and routing, computed from the rig's own histogram (no engine run)

Replaying `vk_preload_tier`'s heat rank against `~/.glm53_explain.bin` (12 960
entries, 7 754 non-zero) reproduces the served tier exactly (dev0 1 248, dev2
1 695, dev3 1 695 = 4 638 of 12 096) and gives **177.6 non-resident experts per
layer (min 65, max 220), 7 458 in total = 105.6 GB**, with a usage-weighted
resident share of **0.8934** — so the non-resident set is **10.66 % of routed
calls**, not the 21 % plan §8.1 still quotes (that predates this tier).

The design note could only bracket the number that actually matters, the
**distinct** non-resident experts a chunk needs per layer: 73.5 (histogram
model) to 163 (uniform-within-cold upper bound) at chunk 512. The engine now
counts it (`[STREAM]` line, `COLI_TIMERS=1`, both arms). **Measured: 140.5 per
layer-chunk at chunk 512** (76 693 over 546 prefill MoE calls, 6 327-token
prompt) = 83.6 GB per chunk = **163 MB/token**. Nearer the upper bound than the
histogram model.

### §F2a — the microbenchmark: the ring belongs in host RAM (this refuted the design)

`tools/hot-expert/f2_ring_probe.c` via `f2_ring_probe_chain.sh` through
`run_chain.sh` (rig lock only, gateway up and idle before and after, 8 threads
pinned). It links `c/backend_vulkan.c` and calls the engine's own
`coli_vk_ring_*` and `coli_vk_expert_group_issue/2/3`, at GLM's real shapes
(D 4096, I 2048, int4-g64, 14.16 MB/expert), reading the served model's shards
at fixed-seed random offsets. 48 slots per card, three cards, 144 experts =
2.04 GB per wave. Tags `f2rp_09190732` (VRAM only) and `f2rp_09190737` (both).
GB = 1e9.

| | ring in ReBAR VRAM | ring in host RAM |
|---|---:|---:|
| fill, dev0 / dev2 / dev3 alone (GB/s) | 11.938 / 12.699 / 13.116 | 47.969 / 58.396 / 58.434 |
| **fill, three cards (GB/s)** | **16.260** | **58.565** |
| compute only, 1 / 3 / 6 / 12 rows per expert (ms) | 2.513 / 2.961 / 4.864 / 10.206 | 38.937 / 39.428 / 39.973 / 51.944 |
| **wave = fill + compute, 3 rows (ms)** | **103.718** | **74.687** |
| wave, effective GB/s | 19.65 | **27.29** |
| VRAM cost per card | 0.683 GB | **0** |

**A CPU store into write-combined VRAM is not a GPU DMA read over PCIe.**
§PCIE-STREAM's 61–62 GB/s and §VK-STREAM's 59.9–63.3 GB/s are the GPU pulling;
the CPU pushing over the same link manages 16.3 GB/s on three cards. The F2
design was written around a VRAM ring on that mistake and the probe caught it
before any engine code was written. The host ring wins end to end by **1.39×**
and costs no VRAM at all, so the tier, the G6 reserve and the 1 695 caps are
untouched by construction. Compute is flat in rows up to 6 (38.9 → 40.0 ms) —
the streamed experts are weight-bandwidth-bound, not arithmetic-bound, which is
the second reason the chunk wants to be large.

Implementation: two banks of 32 slots per card in host RAM (0.91 GB per card,
2.72 GB total, `COLI_PREFILL_RING_SLOTS`), alternating, so wave w+1's fill runs
while wave w is in flight — the two legs are CPU stores to DRAM against GPU
reads from DRAM, different resources. Wave 0's fill runs in the gap G9 already
opened between issuing the resident groups and joining them.

### §F2b — the oracle (chain `f2_gate_chain.sh`, tag `f209190817`, rc=0, accept_live PASS)

Every arm at the served tier (`preload dev2: 1695`, `dev3: 1695`, `dev0: 1296`
— dev0 holds 48 more than in service because the CLI oracle runs
`COLI_KDA_GPU=0` and does not pay for the KDA slot pool), `GLM53_PREFIX_CKPT=0`,
private `COLI_CKPT_DIR`, 8 threads pinned, a **frozen copy** of the histogram.
Deep packet 6 327 tokens, shallow 2 061.

**The CLI oracle path does not get a usage histogram for free** the way
`ttft_serve.py`'s engine mode does. Without `COLI_USAGE_PATH` the engine prints
`[VK] no usage history loaded — tier empty` and the oracle measures a
configuration that never serves: zero resident experts, streaming moving 100 %
of the routed calls instead of ~11 %. The first F2 oracle ran that way before
it was caught; `f2_gate_chain.sh` now freezes a copy and **refuses** any arm
whose stderr says `tier empty`. `f6a_gate_chain.sh` has the same omission and
its oracle arms also ran tier-empty (harmless there — that item was
bit-identical — but it is the same trap).

| | comparison | result |
|---|---|---|
| **O1** | knob OFF vs the served pristine `15462dc2093b8ad0`, deep **and** shallow | `teacher_forcing` **IDENTICAL**; `GLM53_LOGIT_DUMP_ALL` **BIT-IDENTICAL** (3 919 703 056 bytes = 6 327 × 154 880 f32) at both depths. Prefill 731.3 s vs 729.8 s (0.2 % apart) |
| **O2** | knob ON vs knob OFF (the shipping delta) | `teacher_forcing` DIFFERS; last-token cosine **0.99315324**, max_abs 10.5523, argmax agrees on **6 014 / 6 327** positions (95.05 %) |
| **O3** | knob ON vs `GLM53_EXPERTS_CPU=2` — **placement only, neither side clamps** | `teacher_forcing` **IDENTICAL**; last-token cosine **0.99999998**, max_abs 0.797825, argmax agrees on **2 061 / 2 061** positions |
| **O4** | `GLM53_PREFILL_CHUNK=512`, streaming OFF, vs the default 128 | `teacher_forcing` DIFFERS; last-token cosine **0.99507885**, max_abs 7.23995, argmax agrees on **6 122 / 6 327** positions (96.76 %) |
| **O5** | knob ON at the DEFAULT chunk 128, vs knob OFF — streaming with no chunk change | `teacher_forcing` DIFFERS; last-token cosine **0.99324674**, max_abs 10.5539, argmax agrees on **6 009 / 6 327** positions (94.98 %) |

**O3 is the correctness result: the streamed kernel is right.** Against an
all-CPU reference with the clamp switched off on both sides, streaming every
non-resident expert through the ring changes not one argmax in 2 061 positions
and leaves the greedy prediction line identical. A second run at the same
oracle with an EMPTY tier — i.e. **100 % of routed experts streamed** — also
came back `teacher_forcing` IDENTICAL with cosine 1.00000000 and max_abs
1.94e-4. The ring, the wave schedule, the device assignment and the
accumulation order are numerically sound.

**Where the shipping delta comes from — and the first answer to this was wrong,
so the sequence is written out.** With only O2 and O4 in hand the natural
reading was "the chunk is most of it": O4 alone moves 205 of 6 327 argmaxes
(3.24 %) and O2, which turns both knobs, moves 313 (4.95 %), so the chunk
looked like two thirds of the delta. **O5 refutes that.** Streaming at the
DEFAULT chunk — no chunk change at all — moves **318 (5.02 %)**, *more* than
streaming-and-chunk together:

| | argmax flips of 6 327 | last-token cosine |
|---|---:|---:|
| O4, chunk 512 alone | 205 (3.24 %) | 0.99507885 |
| O5, streaming alone at chunk 128 | **318 (5.02 %)** | 0.99324674 |
| O2, both | 313 (4.95 %) | 0.99315324 |

These are not independent perturbations that add; they are two comparable
nudges to the same near-ties, and the second one buys nothing. So: **the
streaming is the dominant numerics cost and the chunk rides along for free**,
which is the opposite of what O2-and-O4 alone implied. The streaming cost is
the §G13 swiglu-clamp gap arriving on the ~11 % of routed calls that move from
the CPU to the GPU — the known, still-open correctness gap, not a new one; O3
proves the kernel itself adds nothing.

The chunk change is a pure reassociation — `union_ids` is built in
first-appearance order over the whole chunk (`c/glm53.c`), so a token's 8
routed contributions are summed in a different order once the chunk boundary
moves — and the design note predicted it would be ~1e-7 and negligible. **On
its own it is not negligible**: invisible at 1 064 tokens (`teacher_forcing`
identical, max_abs 1.9e-3), 3.24 % of argmaxes at 6 327. The error accumulates
along the sequence, so the depth a reassociation is checked at is load-bearing
and a shallow check here would have reported "free".
