## §M3 (2026-09-22): attention at 256k for Qwen3.8-Flash-Next -- CLOSED with the v2 kernels: a QSA layer is 60 / 92 / 142 µs at 32k / 128k / 256k with the caches streamed from VRAM, 1.7 ms a token for the 12 layers at 256k plus 0.57 ms for the 36 GDN layers; the design's go/no-go (≤ 10-12 ms) passes by 4x. The first cut below (2.6-3.2 ms a layer) is kept as the history of how.

**What the model does at a full-attention layer (12 of 48; GGUF `qwen4exp.attention.compress_ratios` = 4 on layers 3, 7, ..., 47 -- present in the file, verified from the header after a build agent claimed it absent; llama.cpp's F11 numbers ARE QSA numbers):** indexer keys (4 heads x 128, bf16 in the cache) mean-pooled per block of 4 tokens; one query scores all N/4 blocks; the top 2 048 tokens' worth of blocks are selected; dense GQA attention (24 query heads, 2 KV heads x 256, q8_0 K and V) runs over the selected tokens only; sigmoid output gate. The other 36 layers are Gated DeltaNet (48 heads x 128x128 state per sequence). KV added per token from the shapes: 16.1 KB (M0d measured 17.9 KB in service: cache padding and the indexer's per-block bookkeeping).

**Harness.** `tools/hot-expert/m1/m3_attn.hip` (Sonnet, brief `M3-BRIEF-2026-09-22.md`), synthetic caches of the real shapes on one card, one decode query, 100 warm-ups, 1 000 timed, hipEvents; every kernel against an fp32 CPU reference (cos 1.000000 everywhere, the top-k as a set match). Raw `~/bench/m3/m3_20260922_094608.txt`.

| depth | indexer scan µs (GB/s) | top-k 2 048-of-N/4 µs (threshold bisection) | attention over the selected 2 048 µs | QSA layer µs | x12 = attention ms per token |
|---:|---|---|---|---|---|
| 32 768 | 32.6 (257) | 2 050 | 476 | 2 576 | 30.9 |
| 131 072 | 99.5 (337) | 2 097 | 473 | 2 749 | 33.0 |
| 262 144 | 280.8 (239) | 2 070 | 476 | 3 150 | 37.8 |

Gated DeltaNet decode step: 18.5 µs a layer (state 3 MB read + written = 330 GB/s), **0.67 ms a token for 36 layers**, independent of depth.

**What this says.**
1. **Only the indexer scan depends on depth, and it is small:** 67 MB of pooled keys a layer at 256k, 0.28 ms at 239 GB/s here, ~0.09 ms at the bound. The top-k and the sparse attention are constant in depth. **Qwen3.8's attention at 256k is cheap by construction**; llama.cpp's ~8 ms per QSA layer at 257k (§F11-DEPTH: +100 ms a token over 12 layers) is its implementation, not the model.
2. **These first-cut kernels are not the floor.** The top-k (2.05 ms, a bisection over the score range with a full pass per step) and the attention over 2 048 selected tokens (0.48 ms for 2.2 MB of K/V and 25 MFLOP) are each 20-50x above their bytes; a radix-select top-k and a coalesced gather + online-softmax attention are ordinary kernels. Floor from the bytes at 256k: ~0.09 + ~0.03 + ~0.02 = **~0.15 ms a layer, ~2 ms a token**, against the design's go/no-go of 10-12 ms.
3. **The go/no-go is therefore NOT decided by this run**: with these kernels attention is 38 ms a token (fail); with kernels at the bytes it is ~2 ms (pass by 5x). M3 closes when the two kernels are rewritten (Opus-class, commissioned 2026-09-22) and re-measured; until then the >= 40 tok/s projection in design §6 stays labelled projected, and the resident-token projection from §M5 (~8 ms) gets ~2-3 ms of attention and GDN added, not 38.

**M3 v2 (same day, Opus-tier kernels, commits `c9cc39e` and `6f84d53` on `m5-harness`; raw `~/bench/m3/m3_20260922_101426.txt` single-copy and `m3_20260922_102005.txt` rotated).** The three depth kernels were rewritten: indexer scan as one wave32 per pooled block with `uint4` loads (`wave32_block_uint4`); top-k as a single-launch, single-workgroup MSB-first radix select (11+7+7+7 bits, LDS histograms, exact k with a tie counter; `radix_select_11_7_7_7_1wg`) -- **the first cut's 2 ms was a HOST-driven bisection with a `hipMemcpy` per round, so the first-cut layer number was host latency, not GPU work**; sparse attention as a flash-style split kernel, one workgroup of 12 waves (the 12 query heads sharing a KV head) per 64-token chunk so each gathered q8_0 K/V row crosses VRAM once, online softmax, a combine kernel with the sigmoid gate (`flash_split_wave_per_head`). No spills (VGPR 35/26/49). The oracles are unchanged and pass everywhere (cos 1.000000, set match 1, 13 of 13).

The single-copy run read 2.3 TB/s on the 256k indexer scan -- the 67 MB key array stayed in the 96 MB Infinity Cache across the 1 000 iterations -- so the closing run rotates 12 independent copies of every cache a depth kernel reads (805 MB of pooled keys per cycle at 256k; `--rotate 12`), which is what 12 layers do in one token. The attention's gather touches ~2.2 MB of a 285 MB copy, so its 38 µs remains partly cached (an upper bound on cache help, not on the kernel); the top-k reads the score array the scan just wrote, as in service.

| depth | indexer scan µs (GB/s, streamed) | top-k µs | sparse attention µs | QSA layer µs | x12 ms a token |
|---:|---|---|---|---|---|
| 32 768 | 14.8 (565) | 14.9 | 38.5 | 60.4 | 0.73 |
| 131 072 | 45.5 (737) | 19.3 | 38.4 | 92.4 | 1.11 |
| 262 144 | **86.6 (775)** | 28.4 | 37.7 | **141.8** | **1.70** |

GDN decode step 15.7 µs a layer, **0.57 ms a token**. **Attention at 256k, all in: ~2.3 ms a token.** The indexer scan runs at the VRAM bound (775 of 800 GB/s), so the only depth-dependent cost is the bytes of pooled keys, 67 MB a layer at 256k; the KV a token adds is 16.1 KB by the shapes (17.9 measured in service).

**What this closes.** Design §4 go/no-go: M3 ≤ 10-12 ms -- passed at 2.3 ms. llama.cpp's ~8 ms per QSA layer at 257k (§F11-DEPTH) against 0.14 ms here is a 55x gap in the reference engine's attention path; the model's attention is cheap by construction and the kernels to run it at the bytes exist now (`tools/hot-expert/m1/m3_attn.hip`). Projection for the resident Qwen3.8 token at 256k, every term now measured on this hardware: weights ~7.8 ms at the bound (§M5; hipFire-class expert kernels reach 56 % of it at batch 1, §M1, so 9-10 ms is the honest expectation), attention 1.7 + 0.6 ms, boundaries 0.06 ms -> **~10-12 ms a token, 80-100 tok/s at 256k, labelled projected until L0 measures it.**

## §PLE-GATHER (2026-09-22): per-token gather tables (Qwen3.8's 28.8 GB n-gram embedding) belong in HOST RAM, pinned -- 9.5 µs a token cached, 4.2 ms a token if the pages must come from NVMe

**Why this is a rule and not a finding to rediscover.** Qwen3.8-Flash-Next carries `per_layer_token_embd.weight` [160 x 320 001 536] IQ4_NL = 28.8 GB, a hashed n-gram table (`ple.ngram_size 3`, 16 hash heads of ~20 M rows each, feeding layer 1). Per token the model reads 16 rows of 160 values (~1.4 KB); nothing else touches the table. llama.cpp keeps it on the CPU by construction (`LLM_TENSOR_LAYER_INPUT`, a `GET_ROWS` on the input device, `TENSOR_READ_LAZY`), and every F11 number (24-29 tok/s at ≤128k with all experts on the cards, §F11-M0) was taken with it there. Putting it in VRAM would cost 29 GB of the 72 for 1.4 KB of reads a token; there is no version of this design where that is right.

**Measured on the rig (python, mmap of the shard that holds the table, 16 random rows a token):** page-cached: **9.5 µs a token** (against a 10-40 ms token: nothing). Not cached: **4 243 µs a token** -- 16 random 4 KB page faults from the NVMe at ~265 µs each, which is a 10-40 % tax on every token and the reason a cold model "decodes slowly for a while". At the time of the measurement `fincore` showed only 21 of the 49.8 GB shard in the page cache, because GLM-5.3 (149 GB) was serving and the two models do not fit the 247 GiB together (CLAUDE.md).

**The rule for the Franken engine and for any future model (design §9.1):** a tensor read by a per-token ROW GATHER -- `token_embd`, per-layer / n-gram embedding tables (Gemma-3n/4-style PLE, Qwen3.8's), anything the graph reads with `get_rows` -- lives in host RAM, loaded into an allocated, pinned buffer at start (not left to lazy mmap: the page cache is shared with whatever else runs), and its rows are gathered on the CPU and uploaded with the token. VRAM is for tensors read WHOLESALE per token (trunk, experts, lm_head, KV). The corollary is what made Qwen3.8 resident: 93.7 GB on disk is 64.9 GB of card-side weights once the table is where it belongs.

**The kernel moved later the same evening, at the owner's request: 7.0.0-34-generic -> 7.0.0-38-generic** (`linux-generic`, `linux-image-generic`, `linux-headers-generic`, plus the matching modules, headers, tools and zfs-modules packages; no DKMS modules exist on this box, only `amdgpu-dkms-firmware`). Installed about 21:43-21:45 UTC with the rig idle (no sessions, no engines, no rig lock, cards at 26 MiB, no bench log written for 10 minutes), rebooted 21:46 UTC, back and verified at 21:49 (about 170 s). After the boot: `uname -r` 7.0.0-38-generic, all 3 cards enumerated (Radeon RX 7900 XTX, RADV NAVI31, Mesa 26.0.8, unchanged) and idle at 26 MiB, Ollama sees 3 Vulkan devices, docker/ollama/llama-swap active with nothing failed, the three containers healthy, five endpoints answering, no error-priority kernel messages (two NVMe notices, `unchecked data buffer` and `No UUID available`, are warnings), `dockerd`/`containerd` idle after the Netdata fix. **No measurement was taken on 7.0.0-38**: every page-fault, DRAM-bandwidth and per-token number above this section was measured on 7.0.0-34 or older, so re-baseline before comparing. (Done the same night for the Franken engine's Qwen3.8 path and M4 streaming: §BASELINE-7.0.0-38 below; nothing else was re-baselined.) The 7.0.0-34 and 7.0.0-31 kernels stay installed as GRUB fallbacks (choose from the boot menu, console or BMC needed).

**Deliberately not moved:** the 42 held ROCm/amdgpu packages, Mesa/RADV (not in the pending list on this box), every engine and model, `~/src/*`.

**Finding: Netdata 2.12.0 loads the Docker daemon.** With every container idle, `dockerd` and `containerd` each sat at about **43 % of one core** (load average 5.4 against a 0.05-0.4 idle before the update). Stopping the Netdata container took both to idle, so Netdata, not Docker 29.8.2, is the cause. The fix that was applied: `/etc/netdata/go.d.conf` (in the `netdataconfig` volume; the file did not exist before) now reads `modules:\n  docker: no`, which switches off the go.d Docker collector. Afterwards `dockerd`/`containerd` no longer appear among the busiest processes and the load average fell from 5.5 (restart burst) to 2.1 within a minute and was still falling. Not proven in isolation: which call of the collector costs the CPU (an attempt to pause the plugin was refused, the process is root-owned). Per-container CPU/memory still come from the cgroups plugin; only the Docker-specific charts are gone. **Undo:** delete that file and `docker restart netdata`.

**Caveat for measurements taken that evening.** The owner started a GLM-5.3-Flash llama-server (HIP container, 3 cards, port 5800, ctx 32768) at 21:28 UTC; the Netdata restart for the fix landed at about 21:30-21:31 during its model load. Treat that run's first minutes as perturbed.

**Rollback material** (all on the rig): old containers stopped but intact as `open-webui-new-prev`, `searxng-prev`, `netdata-prev`; old images tagged `rollback/open-webui-new:2026-10-05`, `rollback/searxng:2026-10-05`, `rollback/netdata:2026-10-05`; `~/backups/2026-10-05/` holds `open-webui-volume.tgz` (608 MB, taken with the container stopped, before the newer Open WebUI could migrate its database), `ollama.bin` + `ollama.lib` (the previous Ollama) and `llama-swap.v249`. Netdata's volumes were not backed up, and 2.12.0 may have migrated them, so do not start `netdata-prev` against them without checking. The `-prev` containers and rollback tags can be removed once a few normal days have passed.

**Unattended upgrades** are enabled with Ubuntu's stock origins (including the `-security` pocket, which carries kernels) and no automatic reboot. Since the same evening `/etc/apt/apt.conf.d/52unattended-upgrades-rig` blacklists `linux-image`, `linux-headers`, `linux-modules`, `linux-generic`, `docker-ce`, `docker-buildx-plugin`, `docker-compose-plugin` and `containerd.io` (regexes from the start of the package name), so a kernel or a Docker release can no longer land in the background and change a baseline unseen; they are updated by hand together with a re-baseline. `unattended-upgrade --dry-run -d` reads the list ("Initial blacklist: ...") and finds nothing to install. Everything else in the security pocket still installs on its own. To remove the policy, delete that file.

## §BASELINE-7.0.0-38 (2026-10-05): first measurements on kernel 7.0.0-38 -- the Franken engine's Qwen3.8 path and M4 streaming land within 3 % of the 7.0.0-34 rows (decode 21.5 / 22.8 ms short, 25.7 / 24.5 ms at 262k depth, 262k prefill 350-366 s, three-card stream 52.3 GB/s); **the kernel moved nothing this path can see, and that is weak evidence about the CPU-bound Colibri paths, which were NOT re-baselined**

**Why.** §RIG-ENV-2026-10-05 moved the kernel 7.0.0-34 -> 7.0.0-38 and stated that no number had been taken on it. This is that baseline, taken first, before any Franken change, so a later move can be told from a kernel move. Run 22:00-22:32 UTC the same evening by the owner's instruction; rig idle, `~/bench/.dev_reserved` set, no gateway, rig lock taken through `run_chain.sh` and released, cards back at 26 MiB afterwards.

**What ran.** franken-engine `main` at `b5cf4e0` (clean tree), built for this as `~/src/franken-engine/franken/decode/franken_decode_base738` (sha256 `70a8a39bfe70a052`, ROCm image `rocm/dev-ubuntu-24.04:7.14.0-full` `439edaa8f0c4`) so the in-service binaries stayed untouched; Qwen3.8-Flash-Next UD-IQ4_XS, `--devices 3 --layers 0-47 --threads 8`, cards at `auto` (PCIe 16 GT/s x16 on all three), THP `madvise`, `numa_balancing=0`, swappiness 60, governor `schedutil`. Page cache warmed first with one sequential read of the three shards (93.68 GB in 38.2 s = **2.45 GB/s**, the first read after the reboot, so cold; not comparable to the 723 MB/s of the 2026-09-10 eviction measurement, which used a different method), `fincore` showing shards 2 and 3 fully resident (46.4 + 40.8). Every row twice in fresh processes except the no-graph short decode (once).

| row (flags) | 7.0.0-38, `b5cf4e0` | nearest 7.0.0-34 row (binary of that day) |
|---|---|---|
| decode, short depth, `--hip-graph 1 --time 32` | **21.497 / 21.538 ms** (46.5 / 46.4 tok/s) | 21.60 / 22.18 (§L0-PERF-2) |
| decode, short depth, `--hip-graph 0` | 22.791 ms (43.9 tok/s), one run | 22.96 / 23.00 (§L0-PERF-2) |
| decode at 262 000 depth, graph off | **25.709 / 25.724 ms** (38.9 tok/s) | 25.82 (§L0-PERF-1), 26.06 (§L0-256K) |
| decode at 262 000 depth, `--hip-graph 1` | **24.492 ms = 40.8 tok/s**, one run | 24.44 ms = 40.9 tok/s (§L0-PERF-2) |
| prefill 262 000, chunk 256, `--gemm-lds 1` | **349.8 s (1.335 ms/token) / 366.2 s (1.398)**; a third sample, from the graph-on run (prompt chunks do not use the graph), 360.5 s (1.376) | 354 s (1.35, §L0-PERF-1); 430 s on the graph binary, put down to the page cache in §L0-PERF-2 |
| prefill 32 768, chunk 256, `--gemm-lds 1` | **1.216 / 1.226 ms/token** (39.8 / 40.2 s) | 1.202 / 1.228 and 1.212 / 1.221 (§L0-PERF-2 bisect) |
| M4, one card alone (7.5 / 11.7 MB pieces) | 27.59-27.67 / 27.85-27.95 GB/s, same on 83, 86 and 48 | 27.7-28.0 (§M4) |
| M4, shared-link pair 83+86 | **36.20 / 36.26 GB/s** (54.8-55.1 ms per 1 GB token each) | 36.2 |
| M4, non-shared pair 48+83 | 55.24 / 55.86 GB/s | 55.9 |
| M4, all three at once | **52.28 / 52.29 GB/s** (7.5 / 11.7 MB); two copy streams a card 52.9-53.0 | 52.2 |

Run to run: the short decode pair differs by 0.2 %, the graph-off 262k decode pair by 0.06 %, the three 262k prefills by **4.7 %** (349.8 to 366.2 s, all the same configuration since prompt chunks do not use the graph), the two M4 passes by under 0.5 % on every row. **Every row is within 3 % of the nearest recorded one and most within 1 %.** Raw logs, `env_*.txt` snapshots and `m4_{a,b}.json` are in `~/bench/base738/` on the rig. The chains are `tools/hot-expert/base738/baseline_chain.sh` and `tools/hot-expert/base738/supplement_chain.sh`, byte-identical (sha256 checked) to the copies that ran from `~/bench/base738/`; the supplement is the baseline chain with its run block replaced by the 32k and graph-on 262k rows, so its log lines still say `baseline_chain`. Launch both through `run_chain.sh` (the first run set `SKIP_WARM=1` on its relaunch; see the findings below).

**Host counters (system-wide `/proc/vmstat` deltas around each run).** Major faults **1-28 a run** (18 133 -> 18 203 over all eight engine runs), direct reclaim 0, `numa_hint_faults` 0 (that one is by configuration, balancing is off, not a finding), minor faults 15.6-17.2 million a run (all processes on the box; nothing to compare them with yet, the earlier records did not log them for this engine).

**What this does and does not say.**
- It says the Qwen3.8 Franken path on three cards, the pinned host-to-card copy path and the M4 link topology (the shared 83+86 upstream link caps at 36 GB/s, the lone 48 card takes the rest) are unchanged by the kernel move **within this run's noise**. It cannot separate the kernel from the code: the comparison rows come from binaries of 2026-09-22/23 and this is the tip, with the DeepSeek and GLM ports in between (the graph was generalised across models; §L5-DS4-STEP1 records Qwen bit-identical through that change, not that its speed was unchanged). Both moved together and the numbers still agree, so neither moved this path by more than the noise above.
- It does **not** re-baseline the numbers §RIG-ENV-2026-10-05 warned about. This path keeps the model on the cards and the gather table in a warm page cache, so it barely touches the kernel's memory-management paths (major faults stay near zero because the cache is warm, not because the kernel is unchanged). **Still on 7.0.0-34 and not re-measured:** the Colibri engines (`glm53`, `qwen38`, `qwen38-vk`) and every page-fault, DRAM-bandwidth and CPU-path number behind them (§Q-REBASE and the `perf/rome-cpu-path` rows), the llama.cpp reference arms, DRAM bandwidth itself, and the `perf` profiles (`linux-perf` is a newer build now). A move in any of those needs its own re-baseline before it is blamed on code.
- There is no same-binary 7.0.0-34 run: going back needs a reboot into the GRUB fallback from the console or BMC. If a number ever has to be attributed to the kernel rather than the code, that is the experiment.

**Tooling findings from this run (both cost a retry, neither touches a number).**
1. `franken_decode` exits **rc 4** ("STEP2 NO-ORACLE") on every timing run without `--oracle`, by design (`franken_decode.cpp:619`). `preflight.sh` treats any non-zero status as a failed smoke and refused the first launch (`~/bench/base738/chain_attempt1_smoke_rc4.log`: the run itself was fine, 23.14 ms a token on all three cards). The older chains never met it because they piped the engine through `grep`, which hides the status. The chain now maps 4 to 0 around the smoke; `preflight.sh` itself is unchanged.
2. `--ctx` must exceed `--time-prefill` plus `--time`: `--ctx 32768 --time-prefill 32768 --time 32` exits 2 with "--ctx 32768 is too small for 32768 + 32 tokens". The 32k row uses the record's own shape (`--time-prefill 32768`, no `--time`).
3. `--time-prefill` does not load the n-gram table resident (`FRANKEN_PLE_RESIDENT` is read only by the serve path, `franken_serve.cpp:883`), so a prefill number from this path is a page-cache measurement: warm and `fincore` first, as above, or it is the §L0-PERF-2 430-second case again.
4. The last environment snapshot of the supplement caught card 48:00.0 at 16 390 MiB a moment after its container exited; it was back at 26 MiB minutes later. A snapshot taken at exit is not an idle reading.

DeepSeek and GLM, taken the same night on the same binary: §BASELINE-7.0.0-38-DS4-GLM below.

## §BASELINE-7.0.0-38-DS4-GLM (2026-10-05): DeepSeek-V4-Flash and GLM-5.3-Flash on the Franken engine, kernel 7.0.0-38 -- DeepSeek within 1.5 % and GLM within 2 % of the 7.0.0-34 rows, GLM's `pf2` gate gives the same 14 of 15 with the same one failure; **nothing the kernel move could touch shows up on these two paths either**

**What ran.** The same binary and environment as §BASELINE-7.0.0-38 (`franken_decode_base738` from `b5cf4e0`, sha256 `70a8a39bfe70a052`; `franken_decode` dispatches on the GGUF's architecture, so one binary runs all three models; cards at `auto`, PCIe 16 GT/s x16). DeepSeek first: one sequential read of the three shards (90.93 GB in 34.0 s = **2.68 GB/s**, cold, close to Qwen's 2.45), a preflight smoke, then eight runs with the commands of `ds4_gpu_gate.sh` `s5-depth` and `s5-prefill` (the gate script itself still points at the removed `~/src/colibri-m1` tree, so the chain carries its commands with the paths replaced): mixed-corpus placement `deepseek_mix`, 20 GB of experts a card, 262 144 cells, chunk 256, the MMLU prose. The LDS trunk GEMM keeps its 1.8x (17.04 / 9.82 = 1.74x, 16.89 / 9.29 = 1.82x; the record 1.8x). Prefill on the snapshot arms is **1.2 % slower** than the record's (mean 16.96 against 16.76); decode on the seven arms that are not the fourth snapshot arm averages **70.1 ms against 68.9 (+1.7 %)**, 14.1-14.5 tok/s, inside §L5-GLM-GPU's 13.6-14.9. Two things in the spread are not explained: the fourth snapshot-DMA arm is high in BOTH records (76.7 now, 75.3 then), so it is a pattern of the plan's order and not a new effect, and **the first `--gemm-lds 1` sample is 5.3-5.7 % above the other two** (9.822 against 9.323 and 9.293). The profiled run's decode (78.4 ms) carries the profiler's cost and is not a decode number.

**Host counters.** The eight DeepSeek runs together: major faults 18 223 -> 18 239 (**16**), direct reclaim 0. The GLM gate window: major faults 18 239 -> 162 679 (**+144 440**) and direct reclaim non-zero for the first time in these baselines, `pgscan_direct` 786 722 and `pgsteal_direct` 715 295 pages (about 2.7 GiB). That is the load reading 147 GB of GLM through the page cache while the cache already held 91 GB at the start of the chain (Qwen's shards) plus DeepSeek's 85 GiB, i.e. memory pressure from the cache mix and not a kernel finding; it is also why the **load time is not comparable** with the 2026-09-25 figure (287 s against 476 s: that run's cache state was not recorded, and a 40 % faster load is not attributed to the kernel). `numa_hint_faults` 0 is by configuration (balancing off).

**What this says and does not.** It says the DeepSeek and GLM paths on three cards, including GLM's pinned 143.7 GB mirror, its three-link miss path and its swap machinery, produce the same numerics (4 of 4 exact configs, the same single failing cosine check with the same min cos) and the same speed within the stated noise on 7.0.0-38. As in §BASELINE-7.0.0-38 it cannot separate the kernel from the code (comparison rows from binaries of 2026-09-24/25, this is the tip), and there is no same-binary 7.0.0-34 run. **Not measured and still on 7.0.0-34:** GLM and DeepSeek at 256k depth and their cold 256k prefill, the served path (`accept_live` skips while the rig is development-reserved), the quality harness, the Colibri engines and every CPU-path / DRAM-bandwidth number behind them, the llama.cpp arms, DRAM bandwidth itself.

**Tooling findings from this run.**
1. `glm5_gpu_gate.sh` prints "GLM5 GPU GATE FAIL (1 of 15 configurations failed)" for the known `c512gl` cosine failure and still exits 0 (the chain logged `glm gate rc=0`); the GPU process itself exits 1. The verdict is the `gate_plan_summary configs=15 ok=14 fail=1` line, not the exit status, and a future run that fails a DIFFERENT config would look the same to a caller that reads only `$?`.
2. `ds4_gpu_gate.sh` cannot run as committed: `D=` names `~/src/colibri-m1`, removed in the 2026-09-25 clean-up. This chain replaced the path; the script is not fixed.
3. The launch used a foreground `ssh ... '<chain> & sleep 90; cat log'`, which held the session's command open until its 30-minute limit (the chain, started with `setsid nohup`, was unaffected). CLAUDE.md's `ssh -n -f rome '...'` form does not have this problem.

## §L5-GLM-CKPT-E2E (2026-10-06): GLM-5.3-Flash on the Franken engine, prefix checkpoints end to end -- **`accept_live` PASS and `accept_ui` PASS on the checkpoint build: a new chat over the 4.5k-token tool block reuses 4 548 of 4 575 tokens and answers in 1.7 s (cold: 41 s); the build is now the served `franken_dec_glm`. Four faults found on the way, none in the engine**

**What ran.** franken-engine `b5cf4e0` as `~/bench/franken_bin/franken_dec_glm.ckpt` (sha256 `15dd3595830f6620`, built 2026-09-25 14:48), brought up with `serve_alt.sh franken-glm` and `FRANKEN_DOCKER_BIN` pointing at it (placement `~/bench/m2/glm`, 17 GB of experts a card, chunk 512, staging, `--gemm-lds 1`, adaptation on, one slot, kernel 7.0.0-38), 2026-10-05 23:59 to 2026-10-06 00:22 UTC. Page cache warm, so first request 3 min after the command (the 2026-09-25 serve test needed 20 min with a cold cache). The rig stayed development-reserved: `accept_live` SKIPS under `~/bench/.dev_reserved`, so `~/bench/glm_ckpt_accept.sh` moved the flag aside for the 2-minute run with a restore trap (serve_alt's keeper held the rig lock meanwhile, so the watchdog could not act); the flag was back at 00:05:04. The `SKIPPED` line in `accept_ui`'s own rig-side step is therefore not the accept_live evidence; the run below is.

**`accept_live` (full), the owner's path through Open WebUI's backend** (`~/bench/glm_ckpt_accept.log`, gateway log `~/bench/serve_alt_franken_glm.log`):

| check | result |
|---|---|
| 1. UI new chat A (cold, tool block captured here) | prompt 4 573, reused 0, **ttft 41.04 s** (prefill 40.44 s = 8.8 ms/token, 10 chunks, saving 8 checkpoints cost 972 ms) |
| 2. UI new chat B, another question over the same tool block | PASS prompt 4 575, **reused 4 548, ttft 1.72 s** (1 chunk, restore 22 ms) |
| 5. a reply with no max_tokens | PASS finish=stop, 352 tokens at 11.79 tok/s |
| 3. API follow-up turn | PASS prompt 169, **reused 146**, 1.72 s; ledger `state=continuation expect_reuse=146 engine_reuse=146 ok` |
| 4. short request behind an abandoned 1 321-token one | PASS answered in 7.5 s (cancelled at 13.63 s of prefill, next request 1.67 s ttft) |
| 2b. ledger invariant | PASS 1 checked, 0 MISMATCH, 0 broken |

**`accept_ui`** (real Chromium on the Mac through `ssh -L 13000:127.0.0.1:3000 rome`): browser A first token on screen **3.57 s**, B **2.31 s**, both answered correctly; `model=glm-5.3-flash` read back from the saved chat. Three more UI chats (the debug runs) reused 4 548 of 4 562 tokens at 1.84-2.94 s ttft. Checkpoint cost: 156 MB of recurrent state each in pinned host buffers (8 kept, 1.24-1.46 GB in all), restore 20-68 ms a request.

**Four faults, all in the harness or its environment, all fixed in this commit unless noted:**
1. **`accept_ui` tested the wrong backend.** Since §RIG-ENV-2026-10-05 Open WebUI has two connections enabled, llama-swap on :8080 and the gateway on :8081, and no `ui.default_models`; the front end's own default became llama-swap's `glm53-flash`. The probe never chose a model, typed into that one, and waited 10 minutes for an answer while the gateway under test saw nothing (Open WebUI's log: "Upstream openai-compatible request failed: HTTP 500 ... upstream command exited prematurely", llama-swap's own wording; it had tried to start a llama-server for the model while the engine held the cards, and failed harmlessly). `ui_probe.mjs --model` opens the page as `/?model=ID`, and the probe now reads which model answered from the saved chat and fails (`wrong_model_answered`) if it is not the requested one; `accept_ui.sh` passes `--model glm-5.3-flash` (override `ACCEPT_UI_MODEL`), and so do `p9_ui_multiturn.sh` and `ui/ui_matrix.sh`. **Any request to `:8080` while the engine owns the cards makes llama-swap try to claim them; a UI default pointing there is a hazard, not just a wrong answer.**
2. **`serve_conformance.py --arch glm` phase 3** sent Qwen's `<|im_start|>` markers (no boundary for this engine) and reported `reused=0 (bar 93)`. franken-engine `63287c7` (local branch `glm-conformance-markers`, not yet pushed) gives GLM its own markers; its docstring no longer says GLM has no checkpoints. Against the checkpoint build phase 1 checks 6/7 (rollback to the chunk boundary, 88 of 91, and the shared prefix surviving an interleaved request) and phase 2 PASS, which the old docstring said were expected to fail. One check, turn B `reused == ledger_expect_reuse`, reads 88 of 94 on this arch: the 4-layer test span generates nonsense tokens and the driver rebuilds the follow-up from the decoded text, which need not re-tokenize identically. The real-text equivalent, accept_live's 2b above, passes, which is the evidence it is the harness. **The fixed driver was re-run the same night (03:09-03:13 UTC, `~/bench/serve_conformance_glmfix.py --arch glm`, checkpoint CPU build): phase 3 now PASSES (a second chat reused 81 of 93 tokens, bar 61; chunk count 3 against a naive 2, allowed by the two boundary markers), phases 1 and 2 as before; the one failing check is turn B above.**
3. **The GLM docker wrapper dropped `FRANKEN_SNAP_*` and `FRANKEN_BOUNDARY_TOKENS`** (not in its pass-through list; the engine's defaults equal the DeepSeek launcher's, so nothing was mis-set, but an override would have vanished). Added on the rig (`~/bench/franken_decode_glm_docker.sh`, backup `.bak-20261006`); `start_franken_glm.sh` exports the knobs explicitly and its comments (it said the engine had no checkpoint reuse and the ledger was a no-op) are corrected.
4. **`serve_alt.sh glm` under the development reservation stopped the engine container but left the Franken gateway listening on :8081** with nothing behind it (`/v1/models` answering, every chat a 500). It now calls `stop_gateway` in that branch; I killed the stray process by hand.

**Promotion.** The checkpoint build is copied over `~/bench/franken_bin/franken_dec_glm` (the previous build kept as `franken_dec_glm.nockpt`, sha256 `e3e77a0d251f3feb`); it passed accept_live and accept_ui as above. Nothing serves on 8081 (reserved).

**Observation, now measured: served decode was 11.4-11.8 tok/s here against 12.7-14.8 in §L5-GLM-SERVE (no-checkpoint build) -- a first-request effect plus noise, not a persistent regression.** `glm_serve_ab_chain.sh` (A,B,B,A through the real gateway and `start_franken_glm.sh`, a fresh engine per arm, three greedy 256-token requests each, `~/bench/glmserve_ab/`, 02:28-02:53 UTC, no compiles on the host): requests 2 and 3 of each arm, **A (no-checkpoint build, franken-engine `b9bd25d`) 13.760 tok/s [13.23-14.27], B (checkpoint build `b5cf4e0`) 13.418 [12.77-14.29]: -2.5 % on means, ranges overlap, NO VERDICT, "did not move"**. The first request of each arm, scored out as the warm-up, differs: **A 14.96 / 14.92, B 12.94 / 12.51** (-14 %, the ranges do not overlap in either pair) and the gap is gone by request 2 (A 14.27 / 14.26, B 13.20 / 12.77), so a freshly started checkpoint build decodes its first request ~2 tok/s slower; cause not isolated (placement is still adapting in request 1 in both builds; the checkpoint build also makes async host copies of recurrent state around request boundaries). In absolute terms it is ~1.9 s on a 256-token reply, once per engine start. Per-request spread inside one arm is up to 1.0 tok/s (A req 2 14.27 vs req 3 13.28), which is the size of the earlier 11.8 vs 12.7-14.8 discrepancy.

**Not run:** GLM at 256k through the gateway, the quality harness on this build (the checkpoint path does not change numerics: the runner gate was bit-identical at 64 and 2 200 tokens, §L5-GLM-CKPT), a multi-turn browser conversation (`p9_ui_multiturn.sh`), more than one slot.

## §M6-SMALLGEMV (2026-10-06): card 0's slow small GEMVs (109 vs 163 GB/s in the engine) are **not the card, not its ordinal, not first touch, not clock ramp, not launch gaps** -- a small-GEMV microbenchmark reads 145-147 GB/s on all three cards in every arm; the deficit is something dev0 does in the real token

Run 00:44-00:54 UTC by `m6_chain.sh` through `run_chain.sh`, rig idle, kernel 7.0.0-38, `~/bench/m6/20261006_004443/`.

**Arms** (five processes: `HIP_VISIBLE_DEVICES` unset, 1,2,0 / 2,0,1 / 2,1,0 so every physical card is ordinal 0 in turn, and one with the cards first-touched in reverse order): each card alone in ascending, reversed and rotated bus order; all three at once from three threads; a 2 s busy warm-up first; a host gap of 50 / 100 / 200 us between launches; the engine's token duty cycle (a burst of 128 GEMVs, a host sync, 15 ms idle) with and without a per-token pageable upload; tiny dependent kernels after each GEMV; an event pair around every launch (the engine's `--profile`); weights spread over 12 GB; the sysfs sampler off. During every timed region each card's `pp_dpm_sclk/mclk/fclk`, `gpu_busy_percent`, power and junction temperature were read (read-only; no sysfs write, no DPM change).

**Verdict (the chain's own line): `follows=none slow_bus=none groups_flagged=0/306 min_ratio=0.866 follows_plain=none(0/147) follows_engine_like=none(0/159) ramp=0 hvd_effective=3/3`.** No arm of any process shows a card more than 15 % behind the fastest on any shape. The one measurable effect: **83:00.0 is the slowest board in most arms by 1-9 %** (hc_down+inject 0.91-0.95 of the fastest solo, 0.87 with all three running), a different vbios/board (`113-3E4710U-O4O`, subsystem 0x471e; 86:00.0 is `115-D702BS0-101`, 0x0506; max sclk 2 371 against 2 431 MHz) -- a quarter of the size of the engine's gap (109 vs 163 GB/s is 0.67 of the fastest; the probe's worst card is 0.87-0.99).

**What this settles and what it leaves.** The engine's card-0 gap needs something the probe lacks: the real ~21 GB address spread (the probe's 12 GB `wide` arm flags 0 of 7 groups), the P2P boundary traffic into and out of dev0, dev0's per-token embedding upload (H2D on its main stream, 6.2 ms of `gap_idle` per prefill token in §14 of `GLM5.md`), the helper streams' ring DMAs landing on it, or the real kernel mix. **Hypothesis (a) physical card and (b) ordinal/position are both refuted; the next evidence is the engine's own device timeline (GLM prefill `--timeline`, queued 2026-10-06), not another microbenchmark.** The Qwen decode path's dev0 has no equivalent timeline yet.

## §L5-GLM-TIMELINE (2026-10-06): GLM prefill device timeline -- **card 0's 8.4 MB embedding upload waits ~3.0 s of every ~4.4 s chunk behind the staging ring's DMAs; the pipeline across cards is gated by it. The host is not late.**

Handoff 2026-09-26 §4 item 3 ("the pipeline between cards", dev0 busy 2.7 of 9.0 ms a token). franken-engine `pf-timeline` (`4fa21bc`, `fa7006f`, `f7ce8fd`, local, not pushed): `--timeline FILE` records, per (chunk, layer, card), device start/end of every class of main-stream, helper-stream and ring-copy work (hipEvents at the profiler's hook points) plus host `steady_clock` spans of every issue call, on ONE clock (two-point sync per card before and after the prompt; error bound 25.8-33.4 us per card, drift <= 1.9 ppm, 0 dropped / 0 unresolved events); the analysis script in franken-engine's `franken/decode/` (stdlib) reports per chunk / link / layer. Chain `~/bench/glm5_timeline_chain.sh` through `run_chain.sh`, 01:08-01:17 UTC, one load (`glm5_gpu_gate.sh timeline`): 8 192 prose tokens, 262 144 cells, chunk 512, `--glm-prefill-stage 1 --adapt-prefill 0 --gemm-lds 1`, no decode; output `~/bench/franken/glm5/pftl/`. CPU-arm checks beforehand (agent, `nice 19`): timeline on vs off bit-identical, 164/164 taps; 136 tokens in chunks of 32 against the pre-change reference 164/164 (203 s).

| arm | prefill ms/token |
|---|---|
| A (timeline off) | 9.427 |
| T (timeline on, chunks 2-7 recorded) | **8.572** |
| B (timeline off) | 9.537 |

A vs B 1.2 %; **T is 9.6 % below their mean (the 6 recorded chunks 25.6 % below an average one): the instrumentation is not free, it changes the schedule, and it makes it FASTER** (extra waits and an empty launch after each wait point). The mechanism below was read from T's chunks, where it is already present at 3 s a chunk; in the off arms it can only be the same or worse. Steady state, chunks 3-7: **period 8.695 ms a token**, stream floor at this byte count 3.47 ms (92.50 GB a chunk at 52 GB/s, M4).

**What the timeline shows (chunks 3-5 means):**
- Card 0's main stream: **`embed_upload` 3 048 ms** of a ~4 430 ms chunk; its real layer work (`layer_a` + `moe_b` + `moe_c`) **1 345-1 408 ms**. The gantt (chunk 4) is `AAAArtArt...` for the first 47 of 160 columns, then `EEEE...` for the rest.
- Card 1: **`upstream_wait` 3 008 ms** (the same stall passing down); card 2: 17 ms; card 2's `boundary_copy` 3.9 ms, card 1's 1.2 ms; `hout_copy` 0.1 ms; `join_wait` 0.3 / 0.5 / 12.6 ms. Critical path over chunks 3-7: **upstream 5 898 us a token**; every ring or DMA cause is under 230 us.
- **The host is NOT late (hypothesis H1a of GLM5.md §14.3 refuted):** `step()` returns in 47-53 ms for chunks 2-4 (a full chunk issued in 50 ms, several chunks ahead of the device), and takes 5.4-5.7 s only in chunks 6-7, where host calls block (`moe_b` 3.1 s in chunk 6, `moe_fork`/`help` 1.4 s each in chunk 7): consistent with the issue side hitting back-pressure from the device being several chunks behind, but what the call blocks inside was not isolated. The embedding gather on the host is 2 ms.
- Links: DMA busy 51 / 73 / 76 % of the window, 125.8 / 126.1 / 210.6 GB over five chunks, **20.8 GB/s aggregate against the 52 GB/s of M4**; 1/2/3 rings copying at once 76/24/0 % of the busy time, so a card never has more than two of its three ring streams moving.

**Mechanism.** The upload is `b0.upload(s0.x, ...)` at the top of `Glm5Runner::step` (glm5_graph.cpp:724): an 8.4 MB (T x 4096 floats; a staged `hipMemcpyAsync` from an 8-slot pinned ring, per the build agent -- the first draft of this record said 12.6 MB pageable) host-to-device copy on card 0's main stream. It is a copy-engine (SDMA) command in the same FIFO as the three ring copy streams' multi-GB staged transfers, each gated on a `used[k]` event; chunk c+1's embedding therefore cannot land until chunk c's ring DMAs drain, card 0 cannot start chunk c+1 until then, and the chunks run strictly one behind another instead of overlapping across cards. This is the same class of stall as the adapt-snapshot read-back of §L5-GLM-LDS / franken-engine `473c5cc` (a copy-engine transfer queued behind staging DMAs), which was fixed by a kernel writing through a host-mapped pointer on the compute queue. **Projection (labelled so): with card 0 free to start the next chunk, the period is the busiest card's work, ~1.8 s a chunk = ~3.5 ms a token, which is also the stream floor; the agent's refinement is dev2's own plus helper compute at ~5.4 ms a token (the routed-expert chunk kernel is L2-bound, §14.3 H3), so the honest expectation is 9.4 -> 5-6 ms a token before the kernel is touched.** A fix is commissioned (`pf-embed-kernel`: the embedding rows through a host-mapped buffer and a kernel on the compute queue, two banks with a completion fence, `--embed-upload-dma 1` restores the old path); DeepSeek's `ds4_graph.cpp:698` has the identical upload and is a candidate after GLM is measured.

**H1b, the hardware-queue test (`GPU_MAX_HW_QUEUES=16` in the container, the same gate, `~/bench/glm5_timeline_chain_hwq.sh`, output `~/bench/franken/glm5/pftl_hwq16/`, 01:19-01:27 UTC):** timeline-off arms **A 8.778 / B 8.863 ms a token against 9.427 / 9.537 in the default environment (-7.0 % on means, ranges 8.78-8.86 vs 9.43-9.54, not overlapping)**, and the timeline-ON arm is no longer faster than the off arms (T 8.830, +0.1 %): the instrumentation's 9.6 % "speed-up" above and this 7 % come from the same place (cross-stream waits mapped onto the default four hardware queues). **Not yet a verdict:** the two chains were run one after the other, not interleaved (CLAUDE.md: an uninterleaved pair has read +20 % for a real +3.9 %), so it needs a chain-level A,B,B,A (default, 16, 16, default) before the knob is set anywhere. **On decode it does nothing (`hwq_ab_chain.sh`, A,B,B,A, 02:18-02:28 UTC, `~/bench/hwq_ab/`):** Qwen3.8 decode at 262k cells with graph replay **A 21.606 ms [21.601-21.610], B 21.602 [21.596-21.609]: overlapping, did not move**; DeepSeek decode in the served configuration (eager, adaptation on) at depth 64 **A 48.011 [47.992-48.031], B 47.940 [47.911-47.968]: -0.1 %**. (The chain's `failures=4` are Qwen's benign exit code 4, which the baseline chain's preflight maps to success.) So whatever the queue count does is specific to prefill's multi-stream copy pattern. **And it is not the lever:** with 16 queues `embed_upload` is still **3 173 ms** a chunk (3 048 default), card 1's `upstream_wait` 3 105 ms, and card 2 now also waits on upstream 2 943 ms (17 ms before): the pipeline is still gated by the upload, the queue count only moves where the rest waits.

**Not run / open:** the stage-order alternatives of §14.3 (2: dev2's load, 3: the expert kernel, 4: ring depth, 5: chunk 1024) stay ranked behind the upload and are re-read from the new timeline after it.

| **eager**, adapt OFF / **adapt ON** | 53.2 / **48.8** |
| graph replay, adapt ON, **`--miss-stage 0`** (misses read in place) | **52.97 / 53.19** |
| graph replay, adapt OFF, `--miss-stage 0` | 53.07 / 53.09 |
| depth probe 64 / 8 192, adapt ON vs OFF, graph replay (`ds4_adapt_decode_chain`) | 89.7 / 92.7 vs 46.8 / 47.2 (+96 % at 8 192) |

Verdicts of the bisect (harness): adapt effect with staged misses **+81.0 % conservative**; router counters **did not move** (-0.9 %, overlapping); adapt effect with in-place misses **+0.0 %**; staged vs in-place with adaptation on **-42.5 %**. The graph is captured once and replayed 52 times in every graph arm (`hip_graph_dev*: captures=1 replays=52`, nodes 973 / 932 / 940 in every arm), so it is not re-capture. **Reading:** adaptation by itself is healthy (eager, it halves the missed bytes and is 8 % faster); graph replay by itself is a 4 % win; the staged miss path by itself is the default and fine. The 40 ms is a three-way interaction, and with adaptation on that interaction needs the host mirror of ALL 256 experts a layer (`Ds4Model` `adapt_` branch: missed experts' table entries point into a mapped mirror of every expert of the layer, where without adaptation the mapped region holds only the missed ones; the sizes were not measured). **Mechanism not isolated** (the next arms would be `--stage-wgs`, a profile of a graph run under `rocprofv3`, and the mirror's page-size / TLB behaviour); the router atomics are exonerated.

**What it means.** (1) **The service is unaffected:** `ds4_serve.cpp` reads `FRANKEN_HIP_GRAPH` with default 0 and `start_franken_ds4.sh` does not set it; the 2026-09-25 serve log reads 17.4-18.5 tok/s with adaptation on (400 tokens at 17.44), the eager regime. Setting `FRANKEN_HIP_GRAPH=1` for DeepSeek would be expected to cost ~40 ms a token (same configuration as the slow arms; not run through the gateway); `start_franken_ds4.sh` now says so next to `FRANKEN_ADAPT`. (2) **Correction to §L5-DS4-STEP5 (and rev 71):** "the 89-102 ms of §L5-DS4-ADAPT was the wrong placement, not depth" is wrong or at best incomplete: the adaptation gates (`ds4_gpu_gate.sh adapt-traj`) ran with `--hip-graph 1`, i.e. in this regime, and a good placement (`deepseek_mix`) with adaptation and graph replay reads 92 ms at depth 53 and at depth 8 192 alike. Depth is still not a cost (47.2 / 47.7 / 48.1 ms, adapt OFF), and neither is the placement; the interaction is. (3) The handoff's table row "DeepSeek ~21 tok/s" is the eager adapt-OFF/graph number; served it is ~17.5 tok/s with the gateway in the loop.

**Not run:** the mechanism (above); GLM and Qwen with graph replay and adaptation (GLM graph replay is off in its served launcher too, Qwen has no adaptation); (the served-configuration A,B,B,A of the shared change was run afterwards: §DS4-SHARED-GATE).

## §L4-LOOKAHEAD-STEP0 (2026-10-06): layer-lookahead hit rate for GLM-5.3 decode -- **one layer ahead predicts 57 % (8k prose) to 70 % (chat) of the routed experts and covers 55-60 % of the missed bytes, against 24-26 % / 13 % for "same as the previous token"; the published ~72 % reproduces on chat text only; the price is ~2 bytes of link traffic per useful byte at k = 8.** Positive, modest; not adopted.

External review point 2 / handoff §3 item 2 / design §3.1. M2 had measured only next-TOKEN reuse (25-30 %). franken-engine `lookahead-probe` (`2dbc38f`, `4501b2e`, local, not pushed; `--lookahead-probe [N]`, off by default and bit-identical when off: 201/201 taps exact on the CPU twin, probe on or off). At layer l after `ffn_norm`, in decode steps, it predicts layer l+lag's routed top-8 and logs, per (token, layer, lag): the actual set, each predictor's set, a 288-bit residency mask and the non-resident bytes of each predicted set. **Predictors:** A = layer l+1's router (sigmoid + `exp_probs_b`, the `g.router` selection rule) applied to layer l's `xn_l`; B = the same on layer l's pre-norm FFN input re-normalised with layer l+1's `ffn_norm`; C = the previous token's routing at layer l+1; D = C plus the top-8 of A; S = the router on layer l+1's TRUE input (unit check). Hidden state for A and B: layer l's FFN-module hyper-connection reduction after attention's `hc_post` (the MoE output does not exist yet when a prefetch would have to start). The extra gemv runs on the host from four downloaded vectors a layer, so a probed run's timing means nothing.

Chain `glm5_lookahead_chain.sh` through `run_chain.sh` (wrapper `glm5_lookahead_run.sh`), 01:51-02:06 UTC, one load: `unit0` (lag 0 and 1, 22-token prompt), `prose8k` (the 8 192-token MMLU prose, chunk 512 staged, 512 settle tokens with adaptation running, then 256 probed decode tokens, positions 8 704-8 959, lags 1 and 2), `chat` (a 696-token chat prompt in the model's template, same flow, positions 1 208-1 463). **Unit check on the GPU path: S equals the actual routing in 10 752 of 10 752 records in both runs and at lag 0 A and B recover it 924 of 924.** Placement was settled to a flat miss rate (prose window means 1.56 / 1.39 / 1.48 / 1.37 GB a token).

**Lag 1, target layers 3-44** (A and B differ by <= 0.4 points everywhere; the simpler A is quoted):

| | prose8k | chat |
|---|---|---|
| baseline missed-expert traffic over the probed layers | **1.451 GB/token**, miss rate 0.362 | **0.980 GB/token**, miss rate 0.244 |
| C, previous token (k = 8): recall / missed bytes covered | 0.241 / 0.129 | 0.264 / 0.126 |
| **A k = 8: recall / missed bytes covered / prefetch bytes against baseline misses** | **0.570 / 0.551 / 1.16x** | **0.696 / 0.600 / 1.14x** |
| A k = 12 | 0.677 / 0.656 / 1.81x | 0.802 / 0.732 / 2.03x |
| A k = 16 | 0.742 / 0.721 / 2.49x | 0.855 / 0.801 / 3.03x |
| D, C + top-8 of A (14-15 experts) | 0.658 / 0.606 / 2.04x | 0.753 / 0.640 / 2.02x |
| A k = 8: useful / wasted GB a token | 0.800 / 0.879 | 0.588 / 0.527 |

**Lag 2** (two layers of lead): A8 recall 0.432 / 0.593 and missed bytes covered 0.424 / 0.492 (prose / chat) at 1.24x / 1.25x the baseline traffic; A16 0.586 / 0.748. Per layer the spread is wide (A8 recall 0.21 at layer 25, 0.83 at layer 34 on prose; layers 3-4 and 17-18 are weak, 34-39 strong).

**What this says.** (1) The next layer's router, run on the current layer's state, is a real predictor, 2.4x (prose) to 2.6x (chat) the previous-token baseline, and the published "~71.6 % one-layer predictability" holds on this model for chat-shaped text (69.6 %) and not for dense technical prose (57.0 %). (2) k buys coverage at a steep price: 8 -> 16 adds 17-20 points of coverage and ~1.9 GB of extra traffic a token (both runs); at k = 8 precision is ~0.5, i.e. **about two bytes crossed for every useful one**. (3) A prefetcher covers at most the missed bytes of the experts it predicts: at k = 8 ~55-60 % of the 1.0-1.45 GB a token, the rest is still fetched on demand, so total link traffic would be ~1.6x today's (prose: 1.679 prefetched + 0.651 still missed, against 1.451).

**Projection, labelled as one.** The probe says what can be predicted, not what can be hidden. Decode streams 1.451 GB in ~70 ms a token = ~21 GB/s on average against 52 GB/s aggregate (M4), so the links have room for the wasted 0.88 GB; the ceiling if every useful prefetched byte were hidden behind compute is 0.80 GB / 52 GB/s = ~15 ms of the 70 (<= +27 % tok/s), and one layer of lead (~1.5 ms) carries ~78 MB at the aggregate rate against ~40 MB prefetched a layer at k = 8 (1.679 GB over 42 layers), so lag 1 fits. A realistic gain is a fraction of that and could be negative where prefetch DMA contends with the in-place reads the three-link path already issues. **Next step if wanted (STEP1, not started):** a decode-side prefetch of A's top-8 non-resident experts into a ring on a side stream at layer l for layer l+1, A,B,B,A against the adaptive baseline on settled placement; its oracle is bit-identity (it moves bytes, never numerics). Prefill is out of scope (its staged lists are routing-independent).

**Caveats.** One 8k prose prompt and one chat prompt, 256 tokens each, adaptation still moving the placement a little (the window miss rates drift 1.56 -> 1.37 GB a token); the predictor arithmetic is on the host (GPU sums in another order: the unit check shows no set difference in 21 504 records); probed timing is meaningless; the CPU-twin hint (A8 recall 0.70, layers 3-11, 20 tokens, 12 % resident) was a plumbing check and over-read this.

| `--timeline` on the new path | 8.266 (period 8.373 ms a token, chunks 3-7) | |

**What the new timeline shows (chunks 3-5, ms per chunk; the old path in brackets):** `embed_upload` **0.4** [3 048]; card 0's `moe_b` **3 592** (with `layer_a` 668 and `moe_c` 3: 4 263 against 1 386 for the three before; the stall is now INSIDE the MoE, waiting on the ring DMA); card 1's `upstream_wait` **2 847** [3 008]; a chunk still takes ~4.2-4.3 s on card 0. Links: DMA busy **74 / 72 / 75 %** of the window, **125.7 / 125.9 / 210.3 GB, 5.9 / 5.9 / 9.8 GB/s on average and 8.0 / 8.2 / 13.1 GB/s while a copy is in flight, 21.5 GB/s aggregate** (20.8 before), against M4's 28 GB/s for one card alone and 52 for all three. Critical path: upstream 5 571 us a token, **own DMA with no recorded cause 5 545 us a token** (new), ring-region 237, link-rate causes under 190. **So the embedding upload was waiting behind the ring DMAs, not holding them up; removing it gave the 3 % it freed and exposed the real limit: the three ring streams of a card move 8-13 GB/s while busy and never more than two at once.** This answers the earlier doubt about the stream floor: 92.4 GB a chunk at the achieved 21.5 GB/s is 4.3 s = 8.4 ms a token, i.e. the prefill is DMA-bound at the achieved rate, and the 3.47 ms floor needs the 52 GB/s of M4.

**Why the engine's copies may be slower than M4's (not tested yet; an m7 microbenchmark is being built to separate them):** M4 cycles a 2 GB pool a card allocated with `hipHostMallocPortable`; the engine reads slab-aligned runs from **42 separate ~4 GB `hipHostMalloc(Mapped | Portable)` allocations, ~144 GB of pinned memory**, on a host with THP `madvise`-only and `AnonHugePages: 0 kB` (read 2026-10-06), i.e. 4 KB pages, one NUMA node (so NUMA is not it). Candidates: source span / page-translation reach, the allocation flags, ~169 MB average copy size against M4's expert-sized pieces, and the copies queueing behind each other on one SDMA engine. **If the span or the page size is the cause, the fix is a hugepage-backed (or smaller, hot) mirror and the projection is the 3.5 ms floor; if not, it is in the ring dependencies (`used[k]` events) and the copy issue order.**

**Where the stall went, read by the build agent from the new timeline (`pfemb/timeline.csv`):** it is now ONE event a chunk on card 0: `own_ready_wait` **2 877 ms, all of it in layer 3 (the first MoE layer)**, card 1's `upstream_wait` 2 858 ms, the three cards busy 33 / 31 / 36 % of the period. The wait is the first own-ring copy of the chunk (198 MB): its `ring_wait` lasts 3 133 ms although the `used[0]` event fired at ~0 ms, and it ends at 3 112 ms, when card 0's helper stream for owner 2 writes back the PREVIOUS chunk's last layer (card 2's main stream ends at 3 141 ms); the copy itself then takes 13 ms. **The old-code timeline with `GPU_MAX_HW_QUEUES=16` shows the other half:** `ring_wait` 0.1 ms but `embed_upload` still 3 215 ms. Reading (the agent's, untested): the queue count frees the ring copies, the kernel path frees the upload, and each alone only moves a cross-chunk dependency that rides the same shared hardware queues / copy FIFO; **the next run is this branch WITH `HWQ=16`** (`HWQ=16 EMB_OUT=... glm5_emb_chain.sh`). Other findings of its read-only survey: no other copy-engine transfer in the GLM prefill loop sits behind the rings on a main stream (boundary P2P 1-4 ms, the in-step downloads only under taps / `log_routing`, the helper packet P2P is on helper streams); **a served-path candidate:** `take_snapshot` -> `save_rec_async` (`glm5_serve.cpp:858`) and `protect_cells` -> `save_kv_async` (`:810`) are `hipMemcpyAsync` D2H on each card's MAIN stream, issued at every snapshot point of a long prefill (~once a 512-token chunk), the same stall class by the 473c5cc evidence and not measured (a pattern fix: host-mapped destinations + a copy kernel); **DeepSeek:** `ds4_graph.cpp:698` has the same upload (plus a hash-ids upload at :704) but no staging ring, so the effect should be smaller; with `Ds4Ops::rows_bank` / `record_fence` / `wait_fence` in place the port is the `step()` edit plus a flag. CPU check part 2 (new path against `s5/base136`) was not run by the agent for lack of a gap in the lock; the GPU gate's exact configs cover the same bit-identity.

**The two fixes together (`HWQ=16 EMB_OUT=.../pfemb_hwq16 ~/bench/glm5_emb_chain.sh`, 03:13-03:26 UTC, same gate, same 10 of 10 pass with the four exact configs bit-identical):** prefill **A (old upload) 8.722 / 8.847, B (kernel) 8.360 / 8.393 ms/token** (A mean 8.785, B mean 8.377, B/A 0.954), the timeline run 8.455 (period 8.591). Against the default environment this is **A 9.506 -> 8.785 (-7.6 %) and B 9.189 -> 8.377 (-8.8 %)**: the 16-queue effect replicates on a second, independent pair of chains, and the two together are **-11.9 % from the original 9.506**. **Decode gets slower with 16 queues: 76.443 / 76.481 (A) and 75.657 / 76.471 (B) against 70.871 / 71.039 and 69.413 / 70.991, +7.8 % on the A means and +8.4 % on the B means** -- so `GPU_MAX_HW_QUEUES=16` is a prefill-for-decode trade on GLM (and moves nothing on Qwen or served DeepSeek decode), not something to set in the service. **The timeline of this configuration is the cleanest picture yet:** the three links are **96 / 96 / 95 % busy**, 2 or 3 rings copying at once (58-66 % / 26-34 % of the busy time), `ring_wait` 2.7-3.1 s a chunk, host issue 0.0 and "hidden" waits 46-72 ms in all (the unrecorded cause of the earlier runs is gone), and **each link still moves only 6.0 / 6.0 / 10.0 GB/s while busy, 20.9 GB/s aggregate** (125.3 / 125.6 / 209.3 GB per five chunks), the critical path is "own DMA at link rate 0" (5 694 us a token) plus upstream. **At 95 % link utilisation the prefill is bound by the rate of the staged DMA itself, ~6 GB/s a link, not by dependencies, issue, queues or the upload; M4 reached 28 GB/s for one card and 52 for three.** Everything above (host-mapped 4 KB-page source spread over ~144 GB, flags, copy size, one copy engine per card) is therefore the question, and the m7 microbenchmark is the next measurement; at 52 GB/s the chunk would take 1.8 s (3.5 ms a token) instead of 4.3 s.

**Decision:** the kernel path stays (default on, old path behind `--embed-upload-dma 1`): bit-exact, never slower, removes a hazard that serialised card 0 behind the DMA queue; it is not yet merged or in service (the served `franken_dec_glm` is the checkpoint build of b5cf4e0 without it). Order of the next GLM prefill work: m7 (host-source DMA rate), then the stage-order items of §14.3 re-read from this timeline.

Two measurements, 03:29-04:00 UTC, rig idle, kernel 7.0.0-38, THP `madvise`-only with `AnonHugePages: 0 kB`, one NUMA node (read-only).

Single changes from E: span 2 / 6.7 / 31.4 / 62.4 GB **51.9 / 52.1 / 52.2 / 52.2**; piece 5 / 14 / 64 MB **51.9 / 52.1 / 51.9**; sequential **52.2**, one contiguous 170 MB run **52.3**, one stream a card **52.3**. **Replay of the engine's own staged lists** (the `glm_stage_cards` 11-slot pattern, batches of 17 / 18 / 12 slabs on the two sharing cards and the lone one; ~15 separate 11.67 MB `hipMemcpyAsync` calls and one event per batch): plain copy **57.6**, with events **57.8**, gated by `used[k]`/`ready[k]` with no-op consumers **57.6 / 57.5**, with the timeline's event pairs **58.2 GB/s aggregate; while a copy is in flight 17.1 / 17.1 / 27.6 GB/s a link, against 10.1 / 7.3 / 12.4 in the engine**. **Contention:** a VRAM-streaming kernel (852 GB/s, 916.7 alone) beside the copies: E 51.5, the engine replay 57.7 / 56.7 (gated); an ALU-spin kernel: E 46.4. The remaining variants (`P`, `THP`, `REG4K`, `PNC`, `PC`) were not run: the question they answered (does the source matter) was already settled.

**What this settles, with two timeline cross-checks from the existing data (`pfemb/timeline.csv`, chunks 3-6, no GPU):** (1) the source memory, its span, flags, hugepages, copy size, pattern, number of streams, and even the ring's gating events do not slow the copies in isolation; (2) per-copy rates in the engine do not rise when the card's compute is idle (card 1 idle 3.4 GB/s, card 2 idle 5.2, against 7.0 / 11.7 while computing), so generic compute contention is not it either; (3) the engine's per-copy rate is not a function of the ring wait alone (card 2, copies that did not wait: 19.7 GB/s over 130 GB; card 0, copies that waited < 1 ms: 3.3 GB/s over 46 GB), i.e. the same ring structure gives very different rates on different cards. **What the probe does NOT contain and the engine does:** real consumers (the expert kernels of `own_batch` / `help_batch`, ~15-20 ms a region, whose completion events `used[k]` gate the next copy), the helper-stream P2P write-backs on the same cards, the three owners' rings interleaved by the plan, and the ~23.9 GB of a 24 GB card already allocated. **Ring-size sensitivity inside the engine (`glm_ring_ab_chain.sh`, 04:01-04:13 UTC, one GPU process of the `pf-embed-kernel` build, 8 192 prose tokens, chunk 512, staged, swaps held, `--gemm-lds 1`, default environment, palindrome auto / 800 / 400 / 400 / 800 / auto):** prefill **8.889 / 8.965 (auto, ring 1 170 / 1 256 / 832 MB a card), 8.859 / 8.963 (800 MB), 8.903 / 8.932 (400 MB) ms/token** -- flat within 1 % from a ring a third the size to the auto one. **The ring depth, and so the VRAM spent on it, is not a lever, and the DMA is not starved by too few regions.** Together with the probe's 57 GB/s for the same lists, what is left is how the engine's real consumers and the cross-card dependencies interact with the copies. **The expert kernels skipped (`glm_skipmoe_chain.sh`, 04:17-04:27 UTC, a timing-only debug build `franken_decode_glm_dbgmoe` = `pf-embed-kernel` + a per-config `--debug-skip-moe 0|1` on the ops interface that makes `moe_launch` return before `k_glm5_moe`; staging copies, events, trunk and adaptation unchanged; the output is garbage and the plan has no oracle; one GPU process, palindrome normal / skip / skip / normal + a timelined skip run):** prefill **normal 8.832 / 9.150, skipped 6.678 / 6.691 ms/token (-25 %)**, the timelined skipped run 6.613 (period 6.701 ms a token). **The routed-expert GEMMs cost ~2.2 ms a token on the prefill's critical path, and that is the upper bound for any expert-kernel optimisation (the agent's reading of `k_glm5_moe`: it decodes a row again for each of an expert's ~14 assignments and reads a 16 KB x row from L2 each time, ~1.3 TFLOP/s, L2-bound).** In the skipped run the links are **80 / 81 / 80 % busy, 7.4 / 7.4 / 12.3 GB/s on average, 9.0 / 9.1 / 15.3 GB/s while a copy is in flight, 27.0 GB/s aggregate** (21.5 with the expert kernels, 57-58 for the probe's replay of the same lists, 52 for M4): with no expert compute at all the staged DMA still gets about half of what the probe's replay gets, so **the expert kernels explain 21 -> 27 GB/s and a second factor of ~2 remains in what else the engine does beside the copies** (the trunk GEMMs with `--gemm-lds` and the KDA/MLA attention on the same cards, the helper P2P write-backs, the ring/helper event structure; the probe's ALU-spin hog alone cost 11 %). **Where the GLM prefill stands, in numbers:** 9.5 ms a token originally; -3 % from the embedding kernel, -8 % more from 16 hardware queues (at +8 % decode cost); a free expert kernel would give 6.7; a DMA at M4's rate would bound the chunk at 3.5 ms a token. **Next measurements, in order:** a debug skip of the trunk's heavy kernels as well (the pure staging-and-events skeleton: if the links then reach the probe's 57 GB/s, any compute slows them and the fix is scheduling or kernel efficiency; if not, the structure of the engine's copy issue is the cause), an m7 arm with consumer kernels shaped like the engine's trunk GEMM, then the helper P2P traffic; independently, a better routed-expert chunk kernel is worth up to the 25 %.
